items.passage:
[Prose extract: The walk to school]
For nine years I walked my younger brother to school. We took the same route every morning — past the church, past the garage, past the small shop where the woman who sold bread sometimes called out that there were still warm rolls. I learned, during those nine years, almost everything I know about him. Not from the things he said, which were the usual things a younger brother says on the way to school, but from the spaces between them. From what he asked about and what he did not. From which days he wanted to walk close to me and which days he wanted to trail a few paces behind. From whether his small hand was tight around mine or loose. He did not know I was learning him. I do not think he would have walked in the same way if he had known. When the time came that I had to leave for university and the walking ended, my mother thanked me for it, as if it had been a kindness I had done. It had not been a kindness. It had been an education, and the teacher had been my brother, and the lessons had been the small adjustments he made each morning when he thought no one was studying him. It seemed unfair to accept thanks for what I had, in fact, received.

items.passage:
[Poem: Names]
My grandmother gave me three names.
The first, my school name, was the one she did not choose.
The second, my home name, was the one she did.
The third she gave me on a Tuesday afternoon
when I was nine and we were peeling beans together
on the back step, and she did not tell me
what it meant, only that I should not say it aloud
until I was older, and not even then
unless I needed it.

I am older. I have not yet needed it.
I have considered, on certain bad evenings,
saying it to see what it does.
I have decided, each time, against.
It seems important to keep one thing
she gave me unspent.

She has been dead nineteen years.
I do not know whether the name is a key
or a promise or a warning, only that
she chose it carefully, and that the carefulness
was what she meant me to remember
long after the syllables themselves
had become — as they are, now, becoming —
a thing I could mispronounce.

=== Text 2 ===
[Poem: What is not said]
What is not said in this house is louder
than what is said. The kettle boils. The dog scratches
at the door it is not, today, allowed to open.
My mother turns the page of the newspaper
more deliberately than the page deserves.

We are not, any of us, holding back
a single specific sentence.
We are holding back, between us, a kind of weather —
a low front of unfinished conversations
that we have, by mutual unspoken agreement,
decided not to let break today.

Tomorrow, perhaps. Or next week.
Or, more likely, on the long drive
back from the hospital we will all,
in time, find ourselves driving back from,
the silences turned into a long conversation
that is, by then, more about us than about him.

For now we read. We make tea. We let the dog
stay where she is. The weather sits low
over the table and we agree, with our shoulders,
not to look up at it.

items.passage:
[Poem: Waiting for rain]
There is a way of standing at a window
you only learn during long drought.
It is not, properly speaking, a posture of looking.
There is nothing to be looked at.
The clouds are either there or they are not,
and standing at the window cannot influence which.

It is, rather, a posture of being available —
of refusing, while the matter is undecided,
to be elsewhere.

My father stood at the kitchen window
for an hour each evening of the third dry year.
He did not pray. He was not, I think,
even hoping in the way the word usually means.
He was holding open a space
into which, perhaps, the rain might be permitted
to find him.

When the rain came, it did not find him at the window.
He was outside by then, walking the lane in the dark,
in the wrong shoes, laughing — a sound I had not heard
in two years and would not hear again,
in quite that register, until the year my mother died,
when he made it once more, in private,
for reasons he did not, and I did not ask him to, explain.

items.passage:
[Poem: The late photograph]
It is the last photograph anyone took of him,
and we did not, at the time, know that.
He is at the kitchen table, half-rising,
explaining something with one hand,
the other reaching for a glass already in motion.

I do not remember what he was explaining.
I do not remember whose camera it was,
or who said the small word that turned the heads
of the others at the table, leaving him alone
still looking at his hands.

Looking at it now I cannot decide
whether the photograph is generous
or cruel. Generous, because he is mid-thought,
mid-gesture, alive in the unfinished motion of being him.
Cruel, because the rest of us are turning away
and he does not yet know that this is the moment
the camera will choose to fix.

The light, of course, was beautiful.
The light is almost always beautiful in such photographs.
It is one of the small consolations of being alive,
and one of the small cruelties.
It is both at once, and the photograph does not arbitrate.
It only holds them both in the same frame.

items.passage:
[Poem: The old road]
The old road has been disused for forty years.
Grass has reclaimed it. The fence posts have rotted
or been pulled. The cattle now move across it
as they would across any other patch of veld,
without acknowledging that this was once a route.

Only the trees remember. They were planted
in a long line by my great-grandfather,
who built the road, and who is also disused now —
a name on a stone behind the church,
unvisited except by me, on a single Sunday each year.

I walk the line of the trees in the late afternoon.
Where the road was, the grass is slightly darker,
the soil more compacted than the soil around it.
You can see it if you know to look.
Most people no longer know to look.

I do not know what to do with this knowledge.
I am not a custodian. I am not a historian.
I am a man on a Sunday walk
who notices that the world contains
more lines than the present has chosen to use,
and that the trees, given long enough,
will outlast both the road and me.

[Prose extract: The ride home]
On the drive back from the hospital nobody said the thing everybody was thinking, and by the time we pulled into the driveway it had become too late to say it. The decision had, in the absence of discussion, made itself. My sister would stay with our father in the spare room of her flat. My brother would return to his job. I would, in some sense I had not yet fully accepted, become the person who telephoned the doctor each Friday afternoon to ask the questions our father was no longer willing to ask. None of us had volunteered for these arrangements. None of us had objected to them either. They had been settled by the physics of an hour-long silence in a car. Looking back on that drive now, I cannot decide whether the silence was a kindness — a way of letting us each find our own place without the friction of negotiation — or a cowardice — a way of letting nobody be the person who had named the thing, and so nobody be the person responsible for the arrangement that followed. It was, of course, both. I have stopped pretending to choose between the two. The drive was a kindness and it was a cowardice, and the arrangement that came from it was a fair arrangement and an unjust one, and we have been living with all of these things together for eleven years, and the living has not obliged us to settle them.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The letter]
When the letter from the lawyer arrived, Mama did not open it for three days. She placed it on the dresser between the two photographs of her sisters — the older one in her graduation robes, the younger one at her wedding — and she did not, in the days that followed, glance at it. Or if she did, it was when nobody was watching. We watched, of course. We did not say so. My brother and I had been small children when our father left, and Mama had taught us, without ever phrasing it as a lesson, to give her her silences. The lawyer's letter was one of those silences. We did not know what was in it. We could guess, perhaps. The lawyer was the one our father had used for many years, and the envelope had come from his office, and our father had been ill for some months, and the rest one could put together oneself. On the fourth morning the letter was gone. Mama did not say where. We did not ask. She was thinner that day than she had been the morning before, and she did not eat the bread she had buttered for herself, and after breakfast she put on her good coat and walked down the road to the post office, and she walked back two hours later without the letter, and she went into her room and closed the door, and that was the last of it. I do not know, even now, whether she had opened the letter before she returned it. My brother thinks she did. I think she did not. We have not resolved this, and we will not, because resolving it would require asking Mama, and neither of us, after fifteen years, is willing yet to ask.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The watch]
He had been wearing the watch every day for thirty-one years, and the children, who had grown up with it on his wrist, had assumed it was a watch he had bought himself, or perhaps one that had belonged to his father. It had not occurred to them to ask. The watch was a fact of him, like the way he ate an orange (peel intact, in one long ribbon) or the way he held a newspaper an inch closer than the world's writers seemed to assume. When the watch finally stopped — the small spring inside it surrendering, as small springs do, without ceremony — he took it to the only watchmaker still operating in the town, an elderly man who did not, in fact, repair watches any more but did not, having no other purpose, refuse to look at them. The watchmaker turned it over twice in his hands and asked, without looking up, where he had got it. He answered truthfully: from a woman he had known when he was nineteen. The watchmaker nodded once and said only: she had good taste. They sat for some minutes without speaking, the watch between them on a green cloth. He thought of asking whether the watchmaker had known her. He did not. He took the watch home, set it on his dresser, and did not wear another. His children, when they noticed, asked. He told them what he had told the watchmaker. They did not press for more. They had inherited, from him, this peculiar form of restraint, and they understood, without his having said so, that the rest of the story was not theirs to know.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The confession]
It is not, as I had once imagined, the things she said that I find I cannot forgive. The things she said could be explained — by the late hour, by the wine, by the long year that had preceded them. What I find I cannot forgive is the small smile that accompanied them, which the wine and the lateness could not account for. That smile was considered. It had been arrived at over some period of time, and it had been waiting for an occasion. I do not know how long it had been waiting. I do not know whether she knew, when she smiled it, what it would do. I have decided, in the years since, that this is the more merciful question to ask: not whether she knew, but whether, knowing, she would have smiled it anyway. I think she would. I think she had reached a point at which the smile was the only honest thing she had left, and the saying of the words was almost incidental — a frame for the smile to be placed in. This understanding has not made me forgive her. It has, however, allowed me to stop imagining that the words were the wound. The wound was the smile. The words were only what the smile required, in order to be seen.

=== Text 2 ===
[Poem: Names]
My grandmother gave me three names.
The first, my school name, was the one she did not choose.
The second, my home name, was the one she did.
The third she gave me on a Tuesday afternoon
when I was nine and we were peeling beans together
on the back step, and she did not tell me
what it meant, only that I should not say it aloud
until I was older, and not even then
unless I needed it.

I am older. I have not yet needed it.
I have considered, on certain bad evenings,
saying it to see what it does.
I have decided, each time, against.
It seems important to keep one thing
she gave me unspent.

She has been dead nineteen years.
I do not know whether the name is a key
or a promise or a warning, only that
she chose it carefully, and that the carefulness
was what she meant me to remember
long after the syllables themselves
had become — as they are, now, becoming —
a thing I could mispronounce.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The walk to school]
For nine years I walked my younger brother to school. We took the same route every morning — past the church, past the garage, past the small shop where the woman who sold bread sometimes called out that there were still warm rolls. I learned, during those nine years, almost everything I know about him. Not from the things he said, which were the usual things a younger brother says on the way to school, but from the spaces between them. From what he asked about and what he did not. From which days he wanted to walk close to me and which days he wanted to trail a few paces behind. From whether his small hand was tight around mine or loose. He did not know I was learning him. I do not think he would have walked in the same way if he had known. When the time came that I had to leave for university and the walking ended, my mother thanked me for it, as if it had been a kindness I had done. It had not been a kindness. It had been an education, and the teacher had been my brother, and the lessons had been the small adjustments he made each morning when he thought no one was studying him. It seemed unfair to accept thanks for what I had, in fact, received.

items.passage:
[Poem: After the fire]
We did not save what we had thought we would save.
The photograph albums burned first — not the house,
which lasted longer than the records of it.

On the second day we walked through the rooms
with the borrowed boots of the volunteer crew
and tried to remember what had been in each place.
The mantelpiece. The bookshelf. The cupboard
with the door that had never closed properly.
It was easier to remember the things that hadn't worked.

My mother said, on the bus back to my aunt's,
that fires were either a beginning or an ending
and that anyone who said otherwise had not been in one.
She had been in one before. I did not ask which one
this was — beginning or ending. I think now
she was telling me she did not yet know,
and would not, for a year, and that I should not
expect to know before her.

We slept that night in a house that was not ours.
I could hear my brother breathing in the bed beside me.
I could hear, very faintly, my mother in the next room,
not quite weeping. I lay still. I had become aware,
in a way I had not been aware that morning,
that a life can be in two places at once —
the place where it is happening and the place where
it used to happen — and that the second place
is not entirely available to anyone
who has not learned, by some loss, to look for it.

items.passage:
[Poem: Names]
My grandmother gave me three names.
The first, my school name, was the one she did not choose.
The second, my home name, was the one she did.
The third she gave me on a Tuesday afternoon
when I was nine and we were peeling beans together
on the back step, and she did not tell me
what it meant, only that I should not say it aloud
until I was older, and not even then
unless I needed it.

I am older. I have not yet needed it.
I have considered, on certain bad evenings,
saying it to see what it does.
I have decided, each time, against.
It seems important to keep one thing
she gave me unspent.

She has been dead nineteen years.
I do not know whether the name is a key
or a promise or a warning, only that
she chose it carefully, and that the carefulness
was what she meant me to remember
long after the syllables themselves
had become — as they are, now, becoming —
a thing I could mispronounce.

items.passage:
[Poem: Waiting for rain]
There is a way of standing at a window
you only learn during long drought.
It is not, properly speaking, a posture of looking.
There is nothing to be looked at.
The clouds are either there or they are not,
and standing at the window cannot influence which.

It is, rather, a posture of being available —
of refusing, while the matter is undecided,
to be elsewhere.

My father stood at the kitchen window
for an hour each evening of the third dry year.
He did not pray. He was not, I think,
even hoping in the way the word usually means.
He was holding open a space
into which, perhaps, the rain might be permitted
to find him.

When the rain came, it did not find him at the window.
He was outside by then, walking the lane in the dark,
in the wrong shoes, laughing — a sound I had not heard
in two years and would not hear again,
in quite that register, until the year my mother died,
when he made it once more, in private,
for reasons he did not, and I did not ask him to, explain.

=== Text 2 ===
[Poem: The old road]
The old road has been disused for forty years.
Grass has reclaimed it. The fence posts have rotted
or been pulled. The cattle now move across it
as they would across any other patch of veld,
without acknowledging that this was once a route.

Only the trees remember. They were planted
in a long line by my great-grandfather,
who built the road, and who is also disused now —
a name on a stone behind the church,
unvisited except by me, on a single Sunday each year.

I walk the line of the trees in the late afternoon.
Where the road was, the grass is slightly darker,
the soil more compacted than the soil around it.
You can see it if you know to look.
Most people no longer know to look.

I do not know what to do with this knowledge.
I am not a custodian. I am not a historian.
I am a man on a Sunday walk
who notices that the world contains
more lines than the present has chosen to use,
and that the trees, given long enough,
will outlast both the road and me.

items.passage:
[Poem: The late photograph]
It is the last photograph anyone took of him,
and we did not, at the time, know that.
He is at the kitchen table, half-rising,
explaining something with one hand,
the other reaching for a glass already in motion.

I do not remember what he was explaining.
I do not remember whose camera it was,
or who said the small word that turned the heads
of the others at the table, leaving him alone
still looking at his hands.

Looking at it now I cannot decide
whether the photograph is generous
or cruel. Generous, because he is mid-thought,
mid-gesture, alive in the unfinished motion of being him.
Cruel, because the rest of us are turning away
and he does not yet know that this is the moment
the camera will choose to fix.

The light, of course, was beautiful.
The light is almost always beautiful in such photographs.
It is one of the small consolations of being alive,
and one of the small cruelties.
It is both at once, and the photograph does not arbitrate.
It only holds them both in the same frame.

items.passage:
[Poem: What is not said]
What is not said in this house is louder
than what is said. The kettle boils. The dog scratches
at the door it is not, today, allowed to open.
My mother turns the page of the newspaper
more deliberately than the page deserves.

We are not, any of us, holding back
a single specific sentence.
We are holding back, between us, a kind of weather —
a low front of unfinished conversations
that we have, by mutual unspoken agreement,
decided not to let break today.

Tomorrow, perhaps. Or next week.
Or, more likely, on the long drive
back from the hospital we will all,
in time, find ourselves driving back from,
the silences turned into a long conversation
that is, by then, more about us than about him.

For now we read. We make tea. We let the dog
stay where she is. The weather sits low
over the table and we agree, with our shoulders,
not to look up at it.

items.passage:
[Poem: The old road]
The old road has been disused for forty years.
Grass has reclaimed it. The fence posts have rotted
or been pulled. The cattle now move across it
as they would across any other patch of veld,
without acknowledging that this was once a route.

Only the trees remember. They were planted
in a long line by my great-grandfather,
who built the road, and who is also disused now —
a name on a stone behind the church,
unvisited except by me, on a single Sunday each year.

I walk the line of the trees in the late afternoon.
Where the road was, the grass is slightly darker,
the soil more compacted than the soil around it.
You can see it if you know to look.
Most people no longer know to look.

I do not know what to do with this knowledge.
I am not a custodian. I am not a historian.
I am a man on a Sunday walk
who notices that the world contains
more lines than the present has chosen to use,
and that the trees, given long enough,
will outlast both the road and me.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The letter]
When the letter from the lawyer arrived, Mama did not open it for three days. She placed it on the dresser between the two photographs of her sisters — the older one in her graduation robes, the younger one at her wedding — and she did not, in the days that followed, glance at it. Or if she did, it was when nobody was watching. We watched, of course. We did not say so. My brother and I had been small children when our father left, and Mama had taught us, without ever phrasing it as a lesson, to give her her silences. The lawyer's letter was one of those silences. We did not know what was in it. We could guess, perhaps. The lawyer was the one our father had used for many years, and the envelope had come from his office, and our father had been ill for some months, and the rest one could put together oneself. On the fourth morning the letter was gone. Mama did not say where. We did not ask. She was thinner that day than she had been the morning before, and she did not eat the bread she had buttered for herself, and after breakfast she put on her good coat and walked down the road to the post office, and she walked back two hours later without the letter, and she went into her room and closed the door, and that was the last of it. I do not know, even now, whether she had opened the letter before she returned it. My brother thinks she did. I think she did not. We have not resolved this, and we will not, because resolving it would require asking Mama, and neither of us, after fifteen years, is willing yet to ask.

=== Text 2 ===
[Prose extract: The confession]
It is not, as I had once imagined, the things she said that I find I cannot forgive. The things she said could be explained — by the late hour, by the wine, by the long year that had preceded them. What I find I cannot forgive is the small smile that accompanied them, which the wine and the lateness could not account for. That smile was considered. It had been arrived at over some period of time, and it had been waiting for an occasion. I do not know how long it had been waiting. I do not know whether she knew, when she smiled it, what it would do. I have decided, in the years since, that this is the more merciful question to ask: not whether she knew, but whether, knowing, she would have smiled it anyway. I think she would. I think she had reached a point at which the smile was the only honest thing she had left, and the saying of the words was almost incidental — a frame for the smile to be placed in. This understanding has not made me forgive her. It has, however, allowed me to stop imagining that the words were the wound. The wound was the smile. The words were only what the smile required, in order to be seen.

items.passage:
[Poem: After the fire]
We did not save what we had thought we would save.
The photograph albums burned first — not the house,
which lasted longer than the records of it.

On the second day we walked through the rooms
with the borrowed boots of the volunteer crew
and tried to remember what had been in each place.
The mantelpiece. The bookshelf. The cupboard
with the door that had never closed properly.
It was easier to remember the things that hadn't worked.

My mother said, on the bus back to my aunt's,
that fires were either a beginning or an ending
and that anyone who said otherwise had not been in one.
She had been in one before. I did not ask which one
this was — beginning or ending. I think now
she was telling me she did not yet know,
and would not, for a year, and that I should not
expect to know before her.

We slept that night in a house that was not ours.
I could hear my brother breathing in the bed beside me.
I could hear, very faintly, my mother in the next room,
not quite weeping. I lay still. I had become aware,
in a way I had not been aware that morning,
that a life can be in two places at once —
the place where it is happening and the place where
it used to happen — and that the second place
is not entirely available to anyone
who has not learned, by some loss, to look for it.

items.passage:
[Poem: Names]
My grandmother gave me three names.
The first, my school name, was the one she did not choose.
The second, my home name, was the one she did.
The third she gave me on a Tuesday afternoon
when I was nine and we were peeling beans together
on the back step, and she did not tell me
what it meant, only that I should not say it aloud
until I was older, and not even then
unless I needed it.

I am older. I have not yet needed it.
I have considered, on certain bad evenings,
saying it to see what it does.
I have decided, each time, against.
It seems important to keep one thing
she gave me unspent.

She has been dead nineteen years.
I do not know whether the name is a key
or a promise or a warning, only that
she chose it carefully, and that the carefulness
was what she meant me to remember
long after the syllables themselves
had become — as they are, now, becoming —
a thing I could mispronounce.

items.passage:
[Poem: Waiting for rain]
There is a way of standing at a window
you only learn during long drought.
It is not, properly speaking, a posture of looking.
There is nothing to be looked at.
The clouds are either there or they are not,
and standing at the window cannot influence which.

It is, rather, a posture of being available —
of refusing, while the matter is undecided,
to be elsewhere.

My father stood at the kitchen window
for an hour each evening of the third dry year.
He did not pray. He was not, I think,
even hoping in the way the word usually means.
He was holding open a space
into which, perhaps, the rain might be permitted
to find him.

When the rain came, it did not find him at the window.
He was outside by then, walking the lane in the dark,
in the wrong shoes, laughing — a sound I had not heard
in two years and would not hear again,
in quite that register, until the year my mother died,
when he made it once more, in private,
for reasons he did not, and I did not ask him to, explain.

items.passage:
[Poem: The late photograph]
It is the last photograph anyone took of him,
and we did not, at the time, know that.
He is at the kitchen table, half-rising,
explaining something with one hand,
the other reaching for a glass already in motion.

I do not remember what he was explaining.
I do not remember whose camera it was,
or who said the small word that turned the heads
of the others at the table, leaving him alone
still looking at his hands.

Looking at it now I cannot decide
whether the photograph is generous
or cruel. Generous, because he is mid-thought,
mid-gesture, alive in the unfinished motion of being him.
Cruel, because the rest of us are turning away
and he does not yet know that this is the moment
the camera will choose to fix.

The light, of course, was beautiful.
The light is almost always beautiful in such photographs.
It is one of the small consolations of being alive,
and one of the small cruelties.
It is both at once, and the photograph does not arbitrate.
It only holds them both in the same frame.

items.passage:
[Poem: What is not said]
What is not said in this house is louder
than what is said. The kettle boils. The dog scratches
at the door it is not, today, allowed to open.
My mother turns the page of the newspaper
more deliberately than the page deserves.

We are not, any of us, holding back
a single specific sentence.
We are holding back, between us, a kind of weather —
a low front of unfinished conversations
that we have, by mutual unspoken agreement,
decided not to let break today.

Tomorrow, perhaps. Or next week.
Or, more likely, on the long drive
back from the hospital we will all,
in time, find ourselves driving back from,
the silences turned into a long conversation
that is, by then, more about us than about him.

For now we read. We make tea. We let the dog
stay where she is. The weather sits low
over the table and we agree, with our shoulders,
not to look up at it.

items.passage:
[Poem: The old road]
The old road has been disused for forty years.
Grass has reclaimed it. The fence posts have rotted
or been pulled. The cattle now move across it
as they would across any other patch of veld,
without acknowledging that this was once a route.

Only the trees remember. They were planted
in a long line by my great-grandfather,
who built the road, and who is also disused now —
a name on a stone behind the church,
unvisited except by me, on a single Sunday each year.

I walk the line of the trees in the late afternoon.
Where the road was, the grass is slightly darker,
the soil more compacted than the soil around it.
You can see it if you know to look.
Most people no longer know to look.

I do not know what to do with this knowledge.
I am not a custodian. I am not a historian.
I am a man on a Sunday walk
who notices that the world contains
more lines than the present has chosen to use,
and that the trees, given long enough,
will outlast both the road and me.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The letter]
When the letter from the lawyer arrived, Mama did not open it for three days. She placed it on the dresser between the two photographs of her sisters — the older one in her graduation robes, the younger one at her wedding — and she did not, in the days that followed, glance at it. Or if she did, it was when nobody was watching. We watched, of course. We did not say so. My brother and I had been small children when our father left, and Mama had taught us, without ever phrasing it as a lesson, to give her her silences. The lawyer's letter was one of those silences. We did not know what was in it. We could guess, perhaps. The lawyer was the one our father had used for many years, and the envelope had come from his office, and our father had been ill for some months, and the rest one could put together oneself. On the fourth morning the letter was gone. Mama did not say where. We did not ask. She was thinner that day than she had been the morning before, and she did not eat the bread she had buttered for herself, and after breakfast she put on her good coat and walked down the road to the post office, and she walked back two hours later without the letter, and she went into her room and closed the door, and that was the last of it. I do not know, even now, whether she had opened the letter before she returned it. My brother thinks she did. I think she did not. We have not resolved this, and we will not, because resolving it would require asking Mama, and neither of us, after fifteen years, is willing yet to ask.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The watch]
He had been wearing the watch every day for thirty-one years, and the children, who had grown up with it on his wrist, had assumed it was a watch he had bought himself, or perhaps one that had belonged to his father. It had not occurred to them to ask. The watch was a fact of him, like the way he ate an orange (peel intact, in one long ribbon) or the way he held a newspaper an inch closer than the world's writers seemed to assume. When the watch finally stopped — the small spring inside it surrendering, as small springs do, without ceremony — he took it to the only watchmaker still operating in the town, an elderly man who did not, in fact, repair watches any more but did not, having no other purpose, refuse to look at them. The watchmaker turned it over twice in his hands and asked, without looking up, where he had got it. He answered truthfully: from a woman he had known when he was nineteen. The watchmaker nodded once and said only: she had good taste. They sat for some minutes without speaking, the watch between them on a green cloth. He thought of asking whether the watchmaker had known her. He did not. He took the watch home, set it on his dresser, and did not wear another. His children, when they noticed, asked. He told them what he had told the watchmaker. They did not press for more. items.passage:
[Prose extract: The ride home]
On the drive back from the hospital nobody said the thing everybody was thinking, and by the time we pulled into the driveway it had become too late to say it. The decision had, in the absence of discussion, made itself. My sister would stay with our father in the spare room of her flat. My brother would return to his job. I would, in some sense I had not yet fully accepted, become the person who telephoned the doctor each Friday afternoon to ask the questions our father was no longer willing to ask. None of us had volunteered for these arrangements. None of us had objected to them either. They had been settled by the physics of an hour-long silence in a car. Looking back on that drive now, I cannot decide whether the silence was a kindness — a way of letting us each find our own place without the friction of negotiation — or a cowardice — a way of letting nobody be the person who had named the thing, and so nobody be the person responsible for the arrangement that followed. It was, of course, both. I have stopped pretending to choose between the two. The drive was a kindness and it was a cowardice, and the arrangement that came from it was a fair arrangement and an unjust one, and we have been living with all of these things together for eleven years, and the living has not obliged us to settle them.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The confession]
It is not, as I had once imagined, the things she said that I find I cannot forgive. The things she said could be explained — by the late hour, by the wine, by the long year that had preceded them. What I find I cannot forgive is the small smile that accompanied them, which the wine and the lateness could not account for. That smile was considered. It had been arrived at over some period of time, and it had been waiting for an occasion. I do not know how long it had been waiting. I do not know whether she knew, when she smiled it, what it would do. I have decided, in the years since, that this is the more merciful question to ask: not whether she knew, but whether, knowing, she would have smiled it anyway. I think she would. I think she had reached a point at which the smile was the only honest thing she had left, and the saying of the words was almost incidental — a frame for the smile to be placed in. This understanding has not made me forgive her. It has, however, allowed me to stop imagining that the words were the wound. The wound was the smile. The words were only what the smile required, in order to be seen.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The walk to school]
For nine years I walked my younger brother to school. We took the same route every morning — past the church, past the garage, past the small shop where the woman who sold bread sometimes called out that there were still warm rolls. I learned, during those nine years, almost everything I know about him. Not from the things he said, which were the usual things a younger brother says on the way to school, but from the spaces between them. From what he asked about and what he did not. From which days he wanted to walk close to me and which days he wanted to trail a few paces behind. From whether his small hand was tight around mine or loose. He did not know I was learning him. I do not think he would have walked in the same way if he had known. When the time came that I had to leave for university and the walking ended, my mother thanked me for it, as if it had been a kindness I had done. It had not been a kindness. It had been an education, and the teacher had been my brother, and the lessons had been the small adjustments he made each morning when he thought no one was studying him. It seemed unfair to accept thanks for what I had, in fact, received.

items.passage:
[Poem: After the fire]
We did not save what we had thought we would save.
The photograph albums burned first — not the house,
which lasted longer than the records of it.

On the second day we walked through the rooms
with the borrowed boots of the volunteer crew
and tried to remember what had been in each place.
The mantelpiece. The bookshelf. The cupboard
with the door that had never closed properly.
It was easier to remember the things that hadn't worked.

My mother said, on the bus back to my aunt's,
that fires were either a beginning or an ending
and that anyone who said otherwise had not been in one.
She had been in one before. I did not ask which one
this was — beginning or ending. I think now
she was telling me she did not yet know,
and would not, for a year, and that I should not
expect to know before her.

We slept that night in a house that was not ours.
I could hear my brother breathing in the bed beside me.
I could hear, very faintly, my mother in the next room,
not quite weeping. I lay still. I had become aware,
in a way I had not been aware that morning,
that a life can be in two places at once —
the place where it is happening and the place where
it used to happen — and that the second place
is not entirely available to anyone
who has not learned, by some loss, to look for it.

items.passage:
[Poem: Names]
My grandmother gave me three names.
The first, my school name, was the one she did not choose.
The second, my home name, was the one she did.
The third she gave me on a Tuesday afternoon
when I was nine and we were peeling beans together
on the back step, and she did not tell me
what it meant, only that I should not say it aloud
until I was older, and not even then
unless I needed it.

I am older. I have not yet needed it.
I have considered, on certain bad evenings,
saying it to see what it does.
I have decided, each time, against.
It seems important to keep one thing
she gave me unspent.

She has been dead nineteen years.
I do not know whether the name is a key
or a promise or a warning, only that
she chose it carefully, and that the carefulness
was what she meant me to remember
long after the syllables themselves
had become — as they are, now, becoming —
a thing I could mispronounce.

items.passage:
[Poem: Waiting for rain]
There is a way of standing at a window
you only learn during long drought.
It is not, properly speaking, a posture of looking.
There is nothing to be looked at.
The clouds are either there or they are not,
and standing at the window cannot influence which.

It is, rather, a posture of being available —
of refusing, while the matter is undecided,
to be elsewhere.

My father stood at the kitchen window
for an hour each evening of the third dry year.
He did not pray. He was not, I think,
even hoping in the way the word usually means.
He was holding open a space
into which, perhaps, the rain might be permitted
to find him.

When the rain came, it did not find him at the window.
He was outside by then, walking the lane in the dark,
in the wrong shoes, laughing — a sound I had not heard
in two years and would not hear again,
in quite that register, until the year my mother died,
when he made it once more, in private,
for reasons he did not, and I did not ask him to, explain.

items.passage:
[Poem: The late photograph]
It is the last photograph anyone took of him,
and we did not, at the time, know that.
He is at the kitchen table, half-rising,
explaining something with one hand,
the other reaching for a glass already in motion.

I do not remember what he was explaining.
I do not remember whose camera it was,
or who said the small word that turned the heads
of the others at the table, leaving him alone
still looking at his hands.

Looking at it now I cannot decide
whether the photograph is generous
or cruel. Generous, because he is mid-thought,
mid-gesture, alive in the unfinished motion of being him.
Cruel, because the rest of us are turning away
and he does not yet know that this is the moment
the camera will choose to fix.

The light, of course, was beautiful.
The light is almost always beautiful in such photographs.
It is one of the small consolations of being alive,
and one of the small cruelties.
It is both at once, and the photograph does not arbitrate.
It only holds them both in the same frame.

items.passage:
[Poem: What is not said]
What is not said in this house is louder
than what is said. The kettle boils. The dog scratches
at the door it is not, today, allowed to open.
My mother turns the page of the newspaper
more deliberately than the page deserves.

We are not, any of us, holding back
a single specific sentence.
We are holding back, between us, a kind of weather —
a low front of unfinished conversations
that we have, by mutual unspoken agreement,
decided not to let break today.

Tomorrow, perhaps. Or next week.
Or, more likely, on the long drive
back from the hospital we will all,
in time, find ourselves driving back from,
the silences turned into a long conversation
that is, by then, more about us than about him.

For now we read. We make tea. We let the dog
stay where she is. The weather sits low
over the table and we agree, with our shoulders,
not to look up at it.

items.passage:
[Poem: The old road]
The old road has been disused for forty years.
Grass has reclaimed it. The fence posts have rotted
or been pulled. The cattle now move across it
as they would across any other patch of veld,
without acknowledging that this was once a route.

Only the trees remember. They were planted
in a long line by my great-grandfather,
who built the road, and who is also disused now —
a name on a stone behind the church,
unvisited except by me, on a single Sunday each year.

I walk the line of the trees in the late afternoon.
Where the road was, the grass is slightly darker,
the soil more compacted than the soil around it.
You can see it if you know to look.
Most people no longer know to look.

I do not know what to do with this knowledge.
I am not a custodian. I am not a historian.
I am a man on a Sunday walk
who notices that the world contains
more lines than the present has chosen to use,
and that the trees, given long enough,
will outlast both the road and me.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The letter]
When the letter from the lawyer arrived, Mama did not open it for three days. She placed it on the dresser between the two photographs of her sisters — the older one in her graduation robes, the younger one at her wedding — and she did not, in the days that followed, glance at it. Or if she did, it was when nobody was watching. We watched, of course. We did not say so. My brother and I had been small children when our father left, and Mama had taught us, without ever phrasing it as a lesson, to give her her silences. The lawyer's letter was one of those silences. We did not know what was in it. We could guess, perhaps. The lawyer was the one our father had used for many years, and the envelope had come from his office, and our father had been ill for some months, and the rest one could put together oneself. On the fourth morning the letter was gone. Mama did not say where. We did not ask. She was thinner that day than she had been the morning before, and she did not eat the bread she had buttered for herself, and after breakfast she put on her good coat and walked down the road to the post office, and she walked back two hours later without the letter, and she went into her room and closed the door, and that was the last of it. I do not know, even now, whether she had opened the letter before she returned it. My brother thinks she did. I think she did not. We have not resolved this, and we will not, because resolving it would require asking Mama, and neither of us, after fifteen years, is willing yet to ask.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The watch]
He had been wearing the watch every day for thirty-one years, and the children, who had grown up with it on his wrist, had assumed it was a watch he had bought himself, or perhaps one that had belonged to his father. It had not occurred to them to ask. The watch was a fact of him, like the way he ate an orange (peel intact, in one long ribbon) or the way he held a newspaper an inch closer than the world's writers seemed to assume. When the watch finally stopped — the small spring inside it surrendering, as small springs do, without ceremony — he took it to the only watchmaker still operating in the town, an elderly man who did not, in fact, repair watches any more but did not, having no other purpose, refuse to look at them. The watchmaker turned it over twice in his hands and asked, without looking up, where he had got it. He answered truthfully: from a woman he had known when he was nineteen. The watchmaker nodded once and said only: she had good taste. They sat for some minutes without speaking, the watch between them on a green cloth. He thought of asking whether the watchmaker had known her. He did not. He took the watch home, set it on his dresser, and did not wear another. His children, when they noticed, asked. He told them what he had told the watchmaker. They did not press for more. They had inherited, from him, this peculiar form of restraint, and they understood, without his having said so, that the rest of the story was not theirs to know.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The ride home]
On the drive back from the hospital nobody said the thing everybody was thinking, and by the time we pulled into the driveway it had become too late to say it. The decision had, in the absence of discussion, made itself. My sister would stay with our father in the spare room of her flat. My brother would return to his job. I would, in some sense I had not yet fully accepted, become the person who telephoned the doctor each Friday afternoon to ask the questions our father was no longer willing to ask. None of us had volunteered for these arrangements. None of us had objected to them either. They had been settled by the physics of an hour-long silence in a car. Looking back on that drive now, I cannot decide whether the silence was a kindness — a way of letting us each find our own place without the friction of negotiation — or a cowardice — a way of letting nobody be the person who had named the thing, and so nobody be the person responsible for the arrangement that followed. It was, of course, both. I have stopped pretending to choose between the two. The drive was a kindness and it was a cowardice, and the arrangement that came from it was a fair arrangement and an unjust one, and we have been living with all of these things together for eleven years, and the living has not obliged us to settle them.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The confession]
It is not, as I had once imagined, the things she said that I find I cannot forgive. The things she said could be explained — by the late hour, by the wine, by the long year that had preceded them. What I find I cannot forgive is the small smile that accompanied them, which the wine and the lateness could not account for. That smile was considered. It had been arrived at over some period of time, and it had been waiting for an occasion. I do not know how long it had been waiting. I do not know whether she knew, when she smiled it, what it would do. I have decided, in the years since, that this is the more merciful question to ask: not whether she knew, but whether, knowing, she would have smiled it anyway. I think she would. I think she had reached a point at which the smile was the only honest thing she had left, and the saying of the words was almost incidental — a frame for the smile to be placed in. This understanding has not made me forgive her. It has, however, allowed me to stop imagining that the words were the wound. The wound was the smile. The words were only what the smile required, in order to be seen.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The walk to school]
For nine years I walked my younger brother to school. We took the same route every morning — past the church, past the garage, past the small shop where the woman who sold bread sometimes called out that there were still warm rolls. I learned, during those nine years, almost everything I know about him. Not from the things he said, which were the usual things a younger brother says on the way to school, but from the spaces between them. From what he asked about and what he did not. From which days he wanted to walk close to me and which days he wanted to trail a few paces behind. From whether his small hand was tight around mine or loose. He did not know I was learning him. I do not think he would have walked in the same way if he had known. When the time came that I had to leave for university and the walking ended, my mother thanked me for it, as if it had been a kindness I had done. It had not been a kindness. It had been an education, and the teacher had been my brother, and the lessons had been the small adjustments he made each morning when he thought no one was studying him. It seemed unfair to accept thanks for what I had, in fact, received.

items.passage:
[Poem: After the fire]
We did not save what we had thought we would save.
The photograph albums burned first — not the house,
which lasted longer than the records of it.

On the second day we walked through the rooms
with the borrowed boots of the volunteer crew
and tried to remember what had been in each place.
The mantelpiece. The bookshelf. The cupboard
with the door that had never closed properly.
It was easier to remember the things that hadn't worked.

My mother said, on the bus back to my aunt's,
that fires were either a beginning or an ending
and that anyone who said otherwise had not been in one.
She had been in one before. I did not ask which one
this was — beginning or ending. I think now
she was telling me she did not yet know,
and would not, for a year, and that I should not
expect to know before her.

We slept that night in a house that was not ours.
I could hear my brother breathing in the bed beside me.
I could hear, very faintly, my mother in the next room,
not quite weeping. I lay still. I had become aware,
in a way I had not been aware that morning,
that a life can be in two places at once —
the place where it is happening and the place where
it used to happen — and that the second place
is not entirely available to anyone
who has not learned, by some loss, to look for it.

items.passage:
[Poem: Names]
My grandmother gave me three names.
The first, my school name, was the one she did not choose.
The second, my home name, was the one she did.
The third she gave me on a Tuesday afternoon
when I was nine and we were peeling beans together
on the back step, and she did not tell me
what it meant, only that I should not say it aloud
until I was older, and not even then
unless I needed it.

I am older. I have not yet needed it.
I have considered, on certain bad evenings,
saying it to see what it does.
I have decided, each time, against.
It seems important to keep one thing
she gave me unspent.

She has been dead nineteen years.
I do not know whether the name is a key
or a promise or a warning, only that
she chose it carefully, and that the carefulness
was what she meant me to remember
long after the syllables themselves
had become — as they are, now, becoming —
a thing I could mispronounce.

items.passage:
[Poem: Waiting for rain]
There is a way of standing at a window
you only learn during long drought.
It is not, properly speaking, a posture of looking.
There is nothing to be looked at.
The clouds are either there or they are not,
and standing at the window cannot influence which.

It is, rather, a posture of being available —
of refusing, while the matter is undecided,
to be elsewhere.

My father stood at the kitchen window
for an hour each evening of the third dry year.
He did not pray. He was not, I think,
even hoping in the way the word usually means.
He was holding open a space
into which, perhaps, the rain might be permitted
to find him.

When the rain came, it did not find him at the window.
He was outside by then, walking the lane in the dark,
in the wrong shoes, laughing — a sound I had not heard
in two years and would not hear again,
in quite that register, until the year my mother died,
when he made it once more, in private,
for reasons he did not, and I did not ask him to, explain.

items.passage:
[Poem: The late photograph]
It is the last photograph anyone took of him,
and we did not, at the time, know that.
He is at the kitchen table, half-rising,
explaining something with one hand,
the other reaching for a glass already in motion.

I do not remember what he was explaining.
I do not remember whose camera it was,
or who said the small word that turned the heads
of the others at the table, leaving him alone
still looking at his hands.

Looking at it now I cannot decide
whether the photograph is generous
or cruel. Generous, because he is mid-thought,
mid-gesture, alive in the unfinished motion of being him.
Cruel, because the rest of us are turning away
and he does not yet know that this is the moment
the camera will choose to fix.

The light, of course, was beautiful.
The light is almost always beautiful in such photographs.
It is one of the small consolations of being alive,
and one of the small cruelties.
It is both at once, and the photograph does not arbitrate.
It only holds them both in the same frame.

items.passage:
[Poem: What is not said]
What is not said in this house is louder
than what is said. The kettle boils. The dog scratches
at the door it is not, today, allowed to open.
My mother turns the page of the newspaper
more deliberately than the page deserves.

We are not, any of us, holding back
a single specific sentence.
We are holding back, between us, a kind of weather —
a low front of unfinished conversations
that we have, by mutual unspoken agreement,
decided not to let break today.

Tomorrow, perhaps. Or next week.
Or, more likely, on the long drive
back from the hospital we will all,
in time, find ourselves driving back from,
the silences turned into a long conversation
that is, by then, more about us than about him.

For now we read. We make tea. We let the dog
stay where she is. The weather sits low
over the table and we agree, with our shoulders,
not to look up at it.

items.passage:
[Poem: The old road]
The old road has been disused for forty years.
Grass has reclaimed it. The fence posts have rotted
or been pulled. The cattle now move across it
as they would across any other patch of veld,
without acknowledging that this was once a route.

Only the trees remember. They were planted
in a long line by my great-grandfather,
who built the road, and who is also disused now —
a name on a stone behind the church,
unvisited except by me, on a single Sunday each year.

I walk the line of the trees in the late afternoon.
Where the road was, the grass is slightly darker,
the soil more compacted than the soil around it.
You can see it if you know to look.
Most people no longer know to look.

I do not know what to do with this knowledge.
I am not a custodian. I am not a historian.
I am a man on a Sunday walk
who notices that the world contains
more lines than the present has chosen to use,
and that the trees, given long enough,
will outlast both the road and me.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The letter]
When the letter from the lawyer arrived, Mama did not open it for three days. She placed it on the dresser between the two photographs of her sisters — the older one in her graduation robes, the younger one at her wedding — and she did not, in the days that followed, glance at it. Or if she did, it was when nobody was watching. We watched, of course. We did not say so. My brother and I had been small children when our father left, and Mama had taught us, without ever phrasing it as a lesson, to give her her silences. The lawyer's letter was one of those silences. We did not know what was in it. We could guess, perhaps. The lawyer was the one our father had used for many years, and the envelope had come from his office, and our father had been ill for some months, and the rest one could put together oneself. On the fourth morning the letter was gone. Mama did not say where. We did not ask. She was thinner that day than she had been the morning before, and she did not eat the bread she had buttered for herself, and after breakfast she put on her good coat and walked down the road to the post office, and she walked back two hours later without the letter, and she went into her room and closed the door, and that was the last of it. I do not know, even now, whether she had opened the letter before she returned it. My brother thinks she did. I think she did not. We have not resolved this, and we will not, because resolving it would require asking Mama, and neither of us, after fifteen years, is willing yet to ask.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The watch]
He had been wearing the watch every day for thirty-one years, and the children, who had grown up with it on his wrist, had assumed it was a watch he had bought himself, or perhaps one that had belonged to his father. It had not occurred to them to ask. The watch was a fact of him, like the way he ate an orange (peel intact, in one long ribbon) or the way he held a newspaper an inch closer than the world's writers seemed to assume. When the watch finally stopped — the small spring inside it surrendering, as small springs do, without ceremony — he took it to the only watchmaker still operating in the town, an elderly man who did not, in fact, repair watches any more but did not, having no other purpose, refuse to look at them. The watchmaker turned it over twice in his hands and asked, without looking up, where he had got it. He answered truthfully: from a woman he had known when he was nineteen. The watchmaker nodded once and said only: she had good taste. They sat for some minutes without speaking, the watch between them on a green cloth. He thought of asking whether the watchmaker had known her. He did not. He took the watch home, set it on his dresser, and did not wear another. His children, when they noticed, asked. He told them what he had told the watchmaker. They did not press for more. They had inherited, from him, this peculiar form of restraint, and they understood, without his having said so, that the rest of the story was not theirs to know.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The ride home]
On the drive back from the hospital nobody said the thing everybody was thinking, and by the time we pulled into the driveway it had become too late to say it. The decision had, in the absence of discussion, made itself. My sister would stay with our father in the spare room of her flat. My brother would return to his job. I would, in some sense I had not yet fully accepted, become the person who telephoned the doctor each Friday afternoon to ask the questions our father was no longer willing to ask. None of us had volunteered for these arrangements. None of us had objected to them either. They had been settled by the physics of an hour-long silence in a car. Looking back on that drive now, I cannot decide whether the silence was a kindness — a way of letting us each find our own place without the friction of negotiation — or a cowardice — a way of letting nobody be the person who had named the thing, and so nobody be the person responsible for the arrangement that followed. It was, of course, both. I have stopped pretending to choose between the two. The drive was a kindness and it was a cowardice, and the arrangement that came from it was a fair arrangement and an unjust one, and we have been living with all of these things together for eleven years, and the living has not obliged us to settle them.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The confession]
It is not, as I had once imagined, the things she said that I find I cannot forgive. The things she said could be explained — by the late hour, by the wine, by the long year that had preceded them. What I find I cannot forgive is the small smile that accompanied them, which the wine and the lateness could not account for. That smile was considered. It had been arrived at over some period of time, and it had been waiting for an occasion. I do not know how long it had been waiting. I do not know whether she knew, when she smiled it, what it would do. I have decided, in the years since, that this is the more merciful question to ask: not whether she knew, but whether, knowing, she would have smiled it anyway. I think she would. I think she had reached a point at which the smile was the only honest thing she had left, and the saying of the words was almost incidental — a frame for the smile to be placed in. This understanding has not made me forgive her. It has, however, allowed me to stop imagining that the words were the wound. The wound was the smile. The words were only what the smile required, in order to be seen.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The walk to school]
For nine years I walked my younger brother to school. We took the same route every morning — past the church, past the garage, past the small shop where the woman who sold bread sometimes called out that there were still warm rolls. I learned, during those nine years, almost everything I know about him. Not from the things he said, which were the usual things a younger brother says on the way to school, but from the spaces between them. From what he asked about and what he did not. From which days he wanted to walk close to me and which days he wanted to trail a few paces behind. From whether his small hand was tight around mine or loose. He did not know I was learning him. I do not think he would have walked in the same way if he had known. When the time came that I had to leave for university and the walking ended, my mother thanked me for it, as if it had been a kindness I had done. It had not been a kindness. It had been an education, and the teacher had been my brother, and the lessons had been the small adjustments he made each morning when he thought no one was studying him. It seemed unfair to accept thanks for what I had, in fact, received.

items.passage:
[Poem: After the fire]
We did not save what we had thought we would save.
The photograph albums burned first — not the house,
which lasted longer than the records of it.

On the second day we walked through the rooms
with the borrowed boots of the volunteer crew
and tried to remember what had been in each place.
The mantelpiece. The bookshelf. The cupboard
with the door that had never closed properly.
It was easier to remember the things that hadn't worked.

My mother said, on the bus back to my aunt's,
that fires were either a beginning or an ending
and that anyone who said otherwise had not been in one.
She had been in one before. I did not ask which one
this was — beginning or ending. I think now
she was telling me she did not yet know,
and would not, for a year, and that I should not
expect to know before her.

We slept that night in a house that was not ours.
I could hear my brother breathing in the bed beside me.
I could hear, very faintly, my mother in the next room,
not quite weeping. I lay still. I had become aware,
in a way I had not been aware that morning,
that a life can be in two places at once —
the place where it is happening and the place where
it used to happen — and that the second place
is not entirely available to anyone
who has not learned, by some loss, to look for it.

items.passage:
[Poem: Names]
My grandmother gave me three names.
The first, my school name, was the one she did not choose.
The second, my home name, was the one she did.
The third she gave me on a Tuesday afternoon
when I was nine and we were peeling beans together
on the back step, and she did not tell me
what it meant, only that I should not say it aloud
until I was older, and not even then
unless I needed it.

I am older. I have not yet needed it.
I have considered, on certain bad evenings,
saying it to see what it does.
I have decided, each time, against.
It seems important to keep one thing
she gave me unspent.

She has been dead nineteen years.
I do not know whether the name is a key
or a promise or a warning, only that
she chose it carefully, and that the carefulness
was what she meant me to remember
long after the syllables themselves
had become — as they are, now, becoming —
a thing I could mispronounce.

items.passage:
[Poem: Waiting for rain]
There is a way of standing at a window
you only learn during long drought.
It is not, properly speaking, a posture of looking.
There is nothing to be looked at.
The clouds are either there or they are not,
and standing at the window cannot influence which.

It is, rather, a posture of being available —
of refusing, while the matter is undecided,
to be elsewhere.

My father stood at the kitchen window
for an hour each evening of the third dry year.
He did not pray. He was not, I think,
even hoping in the way the word usually means.
He was holding open a space
into which, perhaps, the rain might be permitted
to find him.

When the rain came, it did not find him at the window.
He was outside by then, walking the lane in the dark,
in the wrong shoes, laughing — a sound I had not heard
in two years and would not hear again,
in quite that register, until the year my mother died,
when he made it once more, in private,
for reasons he did not, and I did not ask him to, explain.

items.passage:
[Poem: The late photograph]
It is the last photograph anyone took of him,
and we did not, at the time, know that.
He is at the kitchen table, half-rising,
explaining something with one hand,
the other reaching for a glass already in motion.

I do not remember what he was explaining.
I do not remember whose camera it was,
or who said the small word that turned the heads
of the others at the table, leaving him alone
still looking at his hands.

Looking at it now I cannot decide
whether the photograph is generous
or cruel. Generous, because he is mid-thought,
mid-gesture, alive in the unfinished motion of being him.
Cruel, because the rest of us are turning away
and he does not yet know that this is the moment
the camera will choose to fix.

The light, of course, was beautiful.
The light is almost always beautiful in such photographs.
It is one of the small consolations of being alive,
and one of the small cruelties.
It is both at once, and the photograph does not arbitrate.
It only holds them both in the same frame.

items.passage:
[Poem: What is not said]
What is not said in this house is louder
than what is said. The kettle boils. The dog scratches
at the door it is not, today, allowed to open.
My mother turns the page of the newspaper
more deliberately than the page deserves.

We are not, any of us, holding back
a single specific sentence.
We are holding back, between us, a kind of weather —
a low front of unfinished conversations
that we have, by mutual unspoken agreement,
decided not to let break today.

Tomorrow, perhaps. Or next week.
Or, more likely, on the long drive
back from the hospital we will all,
in time, find ourselves driving back from,
the silences turned into a long conversation
that is, by then, more about us than about him.

For now we read. We make tea. We let the dog
stay where she is. The weather sits low
over the table and we agree, with our shoulders,
not to look up at it.

items.passage:
[Poem: The old road]
The old road has been disused for forty years.
Grass has reclaimed it. The fence posts have rotted
or been pulled. The cattle now move across it
as they would across any other patch of veld,
without acknowledging that this was once a route.

Only the trees remember. They were planted
in a long line by my great-grandfather,
who built the road, and who is also disused now —
a name on a stone behind the church,
unvisited except by me, on a single Sunday each year.

I walk the line of the trees in the late afternoon.
Where the road was, the grass is slightly darker,
the soil more compacted than the soil around it.
You can see it if you know to look.
Most people no longer know to look.

I do not know what to do with this knowledge.
I am not a custodian. I am not a historian.
I am a man on a Sunday walk
who notices that the world contains
more lines than the present has chosen to use,
and that the trees, given long enough,
will outlast both the road and me.

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The letter]
When the letter from the lawyer arrived, Mama did not open it for three days. She placed it on the dresser between the two photographs of her sisters — the older one in her graduation robes, the younger one at her wedding — and she did not, in the days that followed, glance at it. Or if she did, it was when nobody was watching. We watched, of course. We did not say so. My brother and I had been small children when our father left, and Mama had taught us, without ever phrasing it as a lesson, to give her her silences. The lawyer's letter was one of those silences. We did not know what was in it. We could guess, perhaps. The lawyer was the one our father had used for many years, and the envelope had come from his office, and our father had been ill for some months, and the rest one could put together oneself. On the fourth morning the letter was gone. Mama did not say where. We did not ask. She was thinner that day than she had been the morning before, and she did not eat the bread she had buttered for herself, and after breakfast she put on her good coat and walked down the road to the post office, and she walked back two hours later without the letter, and she went into her room and closed the door, and that was the last of it. I do not know, even now, whether she had opened the letter before she returned it. My brother thinks she did. I think she did not. We have not resolved this, and we will not, because resolving it would require asking Mama, and neither of us, after fifteen years, is willing yet to ask.

[Poem: After the fire]
We did not save what we had thought we would save.
The photograph albums burned first — not the house,
which lasted longer than the records of it.

On the second day we walked through the rooms
with the borrowed boots of the volunteer crew
and tried to remember what had been in each place.
The mantelpiece. The bookshelf. The cupboard
with the door that had never closed properly.
It was easier to remember the things that hadn't worked.

My mother said, on the bus back to my aunt's,
that fires were either a beginning or an ending
and that anyone who said otherwise had not been in one.
She had been in one before. I did not ask which one
this was — beginning or ending. I think now
she was telling me she did not yet know,
and would not, for a year, and that I should not
expect to know before her.

We slept that night in a house that was not ours.
I could hear my brother breathing in the bed beside me.
I could hear, very faintly, my mother in the next room,
not quite weeping. I lay still. I had become aware,
in a way I had not been aware that morning,
that a life can be in two places at once —
the place where it is happening and the place where
it used to happen — and that the second place
is not entirely available to anyone
who has not learned, by some loss, to look for it.

items.passage:
[Poem: Names]
My grandmother gave me three names.
The first, my school name, was the one she did not choose.
The second, my home name, was the one she did.
The third she gave me on a Tuesday afternoon
when I was nine and we were peeling beans together
on the back step, and she did not tell me
what it meant, only that I should not say it aloud
until I was older, and not even then
unless I needed it.

I am older. I have not yet needed it.
I have considered, on certain bad evenings,
saying it to see what it does.
I have decided, each time, against.
It seems important to keep one thing
she gave me unspent.

She has been dead nineteen years.
I do not know whether the name is a key
or a promise or a warning, only that
she chose it carefully, and that the carefulness
was what she meant me to remember
long after the syllables themselves
had become — as they are, now, becoming —
a thing I could mispronounce.

items.passage:
[Poem: What is not said]
What is not said in this house is louder
than what is said. The kettle boils. The dog scratches
at the door it is not, today, allowed to open.
My mother turns the page of the newspaper
more deliberately than the page deserves.

We are not, any of us, holding back
a single specific sentence.
We are holding back, between us, a kind of weather —
a low front of unfinished conversations
that we have, by mutual unspoken agreement,
decided not to let break today.

Tomorrow, perhaps. Or next week.
Or, more likely, on the long drive
back from the hospital we will all,
in time, find ourselves driving back from,
the silences turned into a long conversation
that is, by then, more about us than about him.

For now we read. We make tea. We let the dog
stay where she is. The weather sits low
over the table and we agree, with our shoulders,
not to look up at it.

items.passage:
[Poem: The late photograph]
It is the last photograph anyone took of him,
and we did not, at the time, know that.
He is at the kitchen table, half-rising,
explaining something with one hand,
the other reaching for a glass already in motion.

I do not remember what he was explaining.
I do not remember whose camera it was,
or who said the small word that turned the heads
of the others at the table, leaving him alone
still looking at his hands.

Looking at it now I cannot decide
whether the photograph is generous
or cruel. Generous, because he is mid-thought,
mid-gesture, alive in the unfinished motion of being him.
Cruel, because the rest of us are turning away
and he does not yet know that this is the moment
the camera will choose to fix.

The light, of course, was beautiful.
The light is almost always beautiful in such photographs.
It is one of the small consolations of being alive,

items.passage:
[Prose extract: The watch]
He had been wearing the watch every day for thirty-one years, and the children, who had grown up with it on his wrist, had assumed it was a watch he had bought himself, or perhaps one that had belonged to his father. It had not occurred to them to ask. The watch was a fact of him, like the way he ate an orange (peel intact, in one long ribbon) or the way he held a newspaper an inch closer than the world's writers seemed to assume. When the watch finally stopped — the small spring inside it surrendering, as small springs do, without ceremony — he took it to the only watchmaker still operating in the town, an elderly man who did not, in fact, repair watches any more but did not, having no other purpose, refuse to look at them. The watchmaker turned it over twice in his hands and asked, without looking up, where he had got it. He answered truthfully: from a woman he had known when he was nineteen. The watchmaker nodded once and said only: she had good taste. They sat for some minutes without speaking, the watch between them on a green cloth. He thought of asking whether the watchmaker had known her. He did not. He took the watch home, set it on his dresser, and did not wear another. His children, when they noticed, asked. He told them what he had told the watchmaker. They did not press for more. They had inherited, from him, this peculiar form of restraint, and they understood, without his having said so, that the rest of the story was not theirs to know.

We did not save what we had thought we would save.
The photograph albums burned first — not the house,
which lasted longer than the records of it.

On the second day we walked through the rooms
with the borrowed boots of the volunteer crew
and tried to remember what had been in each place.
The mantelpiece. The bookshelf. The cupboard
with the door that had never closed properly.
It was easier to remember the things that hadn't worked.

My mother said, on the bus back to my aunt's,
that fires were either a beginning or an ending
and that anyone who said otherwise had not been in one.
She had been in one before. I did not ask which one
this was — beginning or ending. I think now
she was telling me she did not yet know,
and would not, for a year, and that I should not
expect to know before her.

We slept that night in a house that was not ours.
I could hear my brother breathing in the bed beside me.
I could hear, very faintly, my mother in the next room,
not quite weeping. I lay still. I had become aware,
in a way I had not been aware that morning,
that a life can be in two places at once —
the place where it is happening and the place where
it used to happen — and that the second place
is not entirely available to anyone
who has not learned, by some loss, to look for it.

items.passage:
[Poem: Names]
My grandmother gave me three names.
The first, my school name, was the one she did not choose.
The second, my home name, was the one she did.
The third she gave me on a Tuesday afternoon
when I was nine and we were peeling beans together
on the back step, and she did not tell me
what it meant, only that I should not say it aloud
until I was older, and not even then
unless I needed it.

I am older. I have not yet needed it.
I have considered, on certain bad evenings,
saying it to see what it does.
I have decided, each time, against.
It seems important to keep one thing
she gave me unspent.

She has been dead nineteen years.
I do not know whether the name is a key
or a promise or a warning, only that
she chose it carefully, and that the carefulness
was what she meant me to remember
long after the syllables themselves
had become — as they are, now, becoming —
a thing I could mispronounce.

items.passage:
[Poem: What is not said]
What is not said in this house is louder
than what is said. The kettle boils. The dog scratches
at the door it is not, today, allowed to open.
My mother turns the page of the newspaper
more deliberately than the page deserves.

We are not, any of us, holding back
a single specific sentence.
We are holding back, between us, a kind of weather —
a low front of unfinished conversations
that we have, by mutual unspoken agreement,
decided not to let break today.

Tomorrow, perhaps. Or next week.
Or, more likely, on the long drive
back from the hospital we will all,
in time, find ourselves driving back from,
the silences turned into a long conversation
that is, by then, more about us than about him.

For now we read. We make tea. We let the dog
stay where she is. The weather sits low
over the table and we agree, with our shoulders,
not to look up at it.
