=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Industry consultancy report]
Across surveyed sectors, organisations that have integrated AI productivity tools report measurable gains in routine task completion — often in the range of fifteen to thirty per cent — but smaller and more variable gains in tasks requiring judgement. Where deployment has been accompanied by deliberate redesign of workflows and reskilling investment, outcomes have been substantially better than where the tools were simply added to existing processes. The most common implementation failure observed is the assumption that productivity gains will accrue automatically from the technology itself, independent of how work is restructured around it.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Union submission to a labour committee]
Members report that the introduction of AI tools has been used, in some cases, as a justification for reduced staffing, narrower job descriptions, and heavier expectations of output per remaining worker. Where AI is deployed as a productivity aid, the results have been positive and the workforce has, on the whole, welcomed it. Where AI is deployed as a headcount-reduction strategy, the results have been negative for both workers and, on members' reports, for service quality. The case for regulation is not a case against AI itself. It is a case against leaving the framing of its deployment entirely to the side that benefits from cost reduction.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Academic analysis]
The literature on technological change and employment is older than the current AI debate and offers consistent patterns. Productivity-enhancing technologies have rarely produced net job losses at the aggregate level, but they have consistently produced redistribution — of work, of wages, and of bargaining power. Whether the redistribution serves the broader economy depends on policy choices made around the technology, not on the technology itself. The debate cast as 'AI versus jobs' is therefore miscast. The genuine question is who captures the gains, under what conditions, and with what obligations to those displaced — a question that applies as readily to the spinning jenny as to a large language model.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Planning economist]
The argument for higher urban density rests on three empirical claims that have, in the main, withstood scrutiny: denser cities use less energy per capita; denser cities support more public transport at lower subsidy per ride; denser cities concentrate the agglomeration effects associated with innovation and wage growth. The argument against — that density produces congestion, pollution, and social strain — tends to confuse correlation with causation. Most of the negative consequences attributed to density are, on closer examination, consequences of under-investment in the infrastructure that density requires.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Letter from a longtime resident]
I have lived on this street for thirty-seven years. When I arrived, it had houses and gardens and children. The planners' argument now is that we should welcome higher buildings because density is good for the environment and for the economy. I do not dispute either claim. I observe that my street has not been consulted on whether the density should happen to it specifically, or on what would happen to the children. I observe that the planners do not live on this street, and will not, when the density is built. The arguments for density may be sound. The way they are being deployed against particular communities is a separate question.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Comparative case study]
Comparison of two mid-sized cities — one that increased density steadily over two decades through neighbourhood-scale changes, and one that introduced high-rise development rapidly in a small number of designated zones — suggests that the pace and geography of densification matter as much as its overall level. The slow-and-distributed city retained stronger neighbourhood ties and showed less displacement of long-standing residents. The rapid-and-zoned city reached its density targets faster but produced greater social friction and more vocal resistance. Both cities are now denser than they were; only one is recognisably the community it had previously been.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Agricultural economist's note]
The case for direct income support during prolonged drought, rather than subsidy of inputs, rests on a consistent finding across reviews of rural policy: subsidies on seed, feed, or water tend to be capitalised into land values and recovered, in time, by landowners rather than by working farmers. Direct cash transfers, by contrast, reach the household and are spent on the household's specific bottleneck. The argument against direct transfers — that they discourage adaptation — is not strongly supported by recent evidence. Adaptation appears to depend on adaptive capacity, which is constrained by liquidity. Constraining liquidity to force adaptation is a strategy that has not, on the evidence, produced the adaptation it was meant to.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: A farmer's testimony]
The third year of drought is when the policy people stop arriving. The first year they come with cameras. The second year with forms. By the third year the only people still arriving are the ones with offers to buy your land. I do not say this because I distrust policy research. I say it because the people writing the research are not the people the research was meant to describe. We have outlived our usefulness as a story. The decisions are being made elsewhere now, by people who have written down what we said in the first year and who have, since then, moved on to whatever the next first year is going to be.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: NGO field report]
Field observations across three drought-affected districts suggest that household-level resilience is shaped less by the size of any single intervention than by the predictability of the support over time. Households that knew, in advance, that a given form of support would continue for at least eighteen months made different decisions than households facing the same support delivered as a one-off. The implication for policy is uncomfortable. Short-term emergency relief, however generous, may produce worse long-term outcomes than smaller but predictable medium-term support — a finding that contradicts the emergency framing under which most current programmes are designed and funded.

Your response (480–680 words) must: (1) cite ALL sources — each contributing real evidence; (2) identify at least 1 point of agreement AND at least 1 point of disagreement between sources, explicitly; (3) develop a SYNTHESISED position that is original — not identical to any single source (similarity ≤0.55); (4) embed evidence with attribution — no quote dumps; (5) use integration framing throughout; (6) achieve inter-source coherence — sources should be in CONVERSATION, not summarised separately; (7) adopt a position that REQUIRES the multi-source evidence — one no single source would support alone.

Task: Write the 480–680 word distinction-level synthesis with original position requiring all sources.

checks.description: ALL sources cited — each contributing real evidence to the synthesised position.
Both at least 1 point of agreement AND at least 1 point of disagreement between sources identified explicitly.
Stated analytical position is original — not identical to any single source (similarity to any one source ≤0.55).
Evidence from sources embedded with attribution — no quote dumps.
Integration framing language used throughout ('taken together', 'while X argues P, Y observes Q', 'all three sources hold X, but').
Inter-source coherence ≥0.85 — sources are in conversation, not separately summarised.
Position adopted is one that requires the multi-source evidence — not a position any single source would support alone.
Length 480–680 words.

answerKey.scoringPhilosophy: Each check scores independently and carries a component tag (reasoning / language / register / format). Diagnostic-only checks (AWL distinction, FK grade, sentence-variety, no-intensifiers, not-formulaic) influence confidence and surface learner suggestions but do NOT contribute to pass/fail. ESL/FAL learners receive band tolerance on language and register components; reasoning component is never penalised for surface grammar weakness, AWL proportion, or readability grade. Distinction-level reasoning expressed in plain language scores fully.
answerKey.passFractionAppliesTo: Sum of non-diagnostic checks only. Diagnostic checks are excluded from the pass fraction calculation.
answerKey.antiPerformativityNote: Performative complexity — long sentences, dense AWL, hedged claims, ornate syntax — does NOT add to the score if reasoning quality is not improved by it. Reasoning quality is the primary signal; stylistic sophistication is secondary.

recoveryMapping.INTER_SOURCE_TENSION_ABSENT_FET: Do your sources agree or disagree? Identify tension or agreement.
recoveryMapping.POSITION_NOT_ORIGINAL_SYNTH_FET: Your position restates one source — what do all sources together reveal?
recoveryMapping.QUOTE_DUMP_SYNTHESIS_FET: Embed each quote in your own sentence.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Industry consultancy report]
Across surveyed sectors, organisations that have integrated AI productivity tools report measurable gains in routine task completion — often in the range of fifteen to thirty per cent — but smaller and more variable gains in tasks requiring judgement. Where deployment has been accompanied by deliberate redesign of workflows and reskilling investment, outcomes have been substantially better than where the tools were simply added to existing processes. The most common implementation failure observed is the assumption that productivity gains will accrue automatically from the technology itself, independent of how work is restructured around it.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Union submission to a labour committee]
Members report that the introduction of AI tools has been used, in some cases, as a justification for reduced staffing, narrower job descriptions, and heavier expectations of output per remaining worker. Where AI is deployed as a productivity aid, the results have been positive and the workforce has, on the whole, welcomed it. Where AI is deployed as a headcount-reduction strategy, the results have been negative for both workers and, on members' reports, for service quality. The case for regulation is not a case against AI itself. It is a case against leaving the framing of its deployment entirely to the side that benefits from cost reduction.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Academic analysis]
The literature on technological change and employment is older than the current AI debate and offers consistent patterns. Productivity-enhancing technologies have rarely produced net job losses at the aggregate level, but they have consistently produced redistribution — of work, of wages, and of bargaining power. Whether the redistribution serves the broader economy depends on policy choices made around the technology, not on the technology itself. The debate cast as 'AI versus jobs' is therefore miscast. The genuine question is who captures the gains, under what conditions, and with what obligations to those displaced — a question that applies as readily to the spinning jenny as to a large language model.

alternateValidPatterns.name: asymmetric-tension
alternateValidPatterns.description: Where all sources broadly agree, an essay may identify points of differing EMPHASIS or differing STAKES as the disagreement — valid where the analysis explains what the differing emphasis would commit each source to.

alternateValidPatterns.name: synthesis-via-tension
alternateValidPatterns.description: Synthesis that names the tension between sources and stakes a position on how to live with it, rather than resolving the tension.

alternateValidPatterns.name: synthesis-via-reframing
alternateValidPatterns.description: Position that reframes the question the sources address, drawing on but not reducing to either source.

alternateValidPatterns.name: synthesis-via-tension-acknowledgement
alternateValidPatterns.description: A synthesis that names a tension between sources and stakes a position on how to live with that tension is original even where the position is partially aligned with one source.

alternateValidPatterns.name: integration-via-shape
alternateValidPatterns.description: Integration may be carried by paragraph-shape (each paragraph cites multiple sources) rather than by integration phrases like 'taken together'.

alternateValidPatterns.name: coherence-via-question-not-claim
alternateValidPatterns.description: Inter-source coherence may be achieved through shared question-frame rather than through agreement on claims — sources in conversation may disagree productively.

alternateValidPatterns.name: distinction-via-third-position
alternateValidPatterns.description: A distinction-position may be a genuinely third position (not a midpoint between sources) that requires all sources to be visible to make sense.

alternateValidPatterns.name: elegant-simplicity
alternateValidPatterns.description: Short, plain, precise sentences are not penalised. Reasoning quality is scored on analytical move per clause, not on word count or vocabulary density.

alternateValidPatterns.name: concise-sophistication
alternateValidPatterns.description: A response at the LOW end of the word range that meets all rubric checks is fully equivalent to a response at the HIGH end.

alternateValidPatterns.name: subtle-interpretation
alternateValidPatterns.description: Interpretations carried by sustained tone, image, or framing — rather than declarative thesis sentences — are valid when the textual basis is identifiable.

alternateValidPatterns.name: restrained-literary-analysis
alternateValidPatterns.description: Few techniques unpacked at depth is preferable to many techniques listed without unpacking.

alternateValidPatterns.name: non-template-reasoning
alternateValidPatterns.description: Non-five-paragraph structure is valid where each rubric function is performed at some location in the essay.

alternateValidPatterns.name: implicit-rebuttal-logic
alternateValidPatterns.description: A rebuttal whose logic is implicit in evidence selection or framing counts as a rebuttal when the implicit claim is recoverable from the prose.

alternateValidPatterns.name: layered-without-overt-labels
alternateValidPatterns.description: Layered reasoning may operate without explicit 'and yet' / 'on the one hand' phrasing where syntactic juxtaposition carries the layering.

alternateValidPatterns.name: unconventional-but-coherent-structure
alternateValidPatterns.description: Circular, fragmented, or structure-as-argument forms are valid where topic-flow and reference clarity sustain coherence.

items.passage:
=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Planning economist]
The argument for higher urban density rests on three empirical claims that have, in the main, withstood scrutiny: denser cities use less energy per capita; denser cities support more public transport at lower subsidy per ride; denser cities concentrate the agglomeration effects associated with innovation and wage growth. The argument against — that density produces congestion, pollution, and social strain — tends to confuse correlation with causation. Most of the negative consequences attributed to density are, on closer examination, consequences of under-investment in the infrastructure that density requires.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Letter from a longtime resident]
I have lived on this street for thirty-seven years. When I arrived, it had houses and gardens and children. The planners' argument now is that we should welcome higher buildings because density is good for the environment and for the economy. I do not dispute either claim. I observe that my street has not been consulted on whether the density should happen to it specifically, or on what would happen to the children. I observe that the planners do not live on this street, and will not, when the density is built. The arguments for density may be sound. The way they are being deployed against particular communities is a separate question.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Comparative case study]
Comparison of two mid-sized cities — one that increased density steadily over two decades through neighbourhood-scale changes, and one that introduced high-rise development rapidly in a small number of designated zones — suggests that the pace and geography of densification matter as much as its overall level. The slow-and-distributed city retained stronger neighbourhood ties and showed less displacement of long-standing residents. The rapid-and-zoned city reached its density targets faster but produced greater social friction and more vocal resistance. Both cities are now denser than they were; only one is recognisably the community it had previously been.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Agricultural economist's note]
The case for direct income support during prolonged drought, rather than subsidy of inputs, rests on a consistent finding across reviews of rural policy: subsidies on seed, feed, or water tend to be capitalised into land values and recovered, in time, by landowners rather than by working farmers. Direct cash transfers, by contrast, reach the household and are spent on the household's specific bottleneck. The argument against direct transfers — that they discourage adaptation — is not strongly supported by recent evidence. Adaptation appears to depend on adaptive capacity, which is constrained by liquidity. Constraining liquidity to force adaptation is a strategy that has not, on the evidence, produced the adaptation it was meant to.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: A farmer's testimony]
The third year of drought is when the policy people stop arriving. The first year they come with cameras. The second year with forms. By the third year the only people still arriving are the ones with offers to buy your land. I do not say this because I distrust policy research. I say it because the people writing the research are not the people the research was meant to describe. We have outlived our usefulness as a story. The decisions are being made elsewhere now, by people who have written down what we said in the first year and who have, since then, moved on to whatever the next first year is going to be.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: NGO field report]
Field observations across three drought-affected districts suggest that household-level resilience is shaped less by the size of any single intervention than by the predictability of the support over time. Households that knew, in advance, that a given form of support would continue for at least eighteen months made different decisions than households facing the same support delivered as a one-off. The implication for policy is uncomfortable. Short-term emergency relief, however generous, may produce worse long-term outcomes than smaller but predictable medium-term support — a finding that contradicts the emergency framing under which most current programmes are designed and funded.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Industry consultancy report]
Across surveyed sectors, organisations that have integrated AI productivity tools report measurable gains in routine task completion — often in the range of fifteen to thirty per cent — but smaller and more variable gains in tasks requiring judgement. Where deployment has been accompanied by deliberate redesign of workflows and reskilling investment, outcomes have been substantially better than where the tools were simply added to existing processes. The most common implementation failure observed is the assumption that productivity gains will accrue automatically from the technology itself, independent of how work is restructured around it.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Union submission to a labour committee]
Members report that the introduction of AI tools has been used, in some cases, as a justification for reduced staffing, narrower job descriptions, and heavier expectations of output per remaining worker. Where AI is deployed as a productivity aid, the results have been positive and the workforce has, on the whole, welcomed it. Where AI is deployed as a headcount-reduction strategy, the results have been negative for both workers and, on members' reports, for service quality. The case for regulation is not a case against AI itself. It is a case against leaving the framing of its deployment entirely to the side that benefits from cost reduction.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Academic analysis]
The literature on technological change and employment is older than the current AI debate and offers consistent patterns. Productivity-enhancing technologies have rarely produced net job losses at the aggregate level, but they have consistently produced redistribution — of work, of wages, and of bargaining power. Whether the redistribution serves the broader economy depends on policy choices made around the technology, not on the technology itself. The debate cast as 'AI versus jobs' is therefore miscast. The genuine question is who captures the gains, under what conditions, and with what obligations to those displaced — a question that applies as readily to the spinning jenny as to a large language model.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Planning economist]
The argument for higher urban density rests on three empirical claims that have, in the main, withstood scrutiny: denser cities use less energy per capita; denser cities support more public transport at lower subsidy per ride; denser cities concentrate the agglomeration effects associated with innovation and wage growth. The argument against — that density produces congestion, pollution, and social strain — tends to confuse correlation with causation. Most of the negative consequences attributed to density are, on closer examination, consequences of under-investment in the infrastructure that density requires.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Letter from a longtime resident]
I have lived on this street for thirty-seven years. When I arrived, it had houses and gardens and children. The planners' argument now is that we should welcome higher buildings because density is good for the environment and for the economy. I do not dispute either claim. I observe that my street has not been consulted on whether the density should happen to it specifically, or on what would happen to the children. I observe that the planners do not live on this street, and will not, when the density is built. The arguments for density may be sound. The way they are being deployed against particular communities is a separate question.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Comparative case study]
Comparison of two mid-sized cities — one that increased density steadily over two decades through neighbourhood-scale changes, and one that introduced high-rise development rapidly in a small number of designated zones — suggests that the pace and geography of densification matter as much as its overall level. The slow-and-distributed city retained stronger neighbourhood ties and showed less displacement of long-standing residents. The rapid-and-zoned city reached its density targets faster but produced greater social friction and more vocal resistance. Both cities are now denser than they were; only one is recognisably the community it had previously been.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Agricultural economist's note]
The case for direct income support during prolonged drought, rather than subsidy of inputs, rests on a consistent finding across reviews of rural policy: subsidies on seed, feed, or water tend to be capitalised into land values and recovered, in time, by landowners rather than by working farmers. Direct cash transfers, by contrast, reach the household and are spent on the household's specific bottleneck. The argument against direct transfers — that they discourage adaptation — is not strongly supported by recent evidence. Adaptation appears to depend on adaptive capacity, which is constrained by liquidity. Constraining liquidity to force adaptation is a strategy that has not, on the evidence, produced the adaptation it was meant to.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: A farmer's testimony]
The third year of drought is when the policy people stop arriving. The first year they come with cameras. The second year with forms. By the third year the only people still arriving are the ones with offers to buy your land. I do not say this because I distrust policy research. I say it because the people writing the research are not the people the research was meant to describe. We have outlived our usefulness as a story. The decisions are being made elsewhere now, by people who have written down what we said in the first year and who have, since then, moved on to whatever the next first year is going to be.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: NGO field report]
Field observations across three drought-affected districts suggest that household-level resilience is shaped less by the size of any single intervention than by the predictability of the support over time. Households that knew, in advance, that a given form of support would continue for at least eighteen months made different decisions than households facing the same support delivered as a one-off. The implication for policy is uncomfortable. Short-term emergency relief, however generous, may produce worse long-term outcomes than smaller but predictable medium-term support — a finding that contradicts the emergency framing under which most current programmes are designed and funded.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Industry consultancy report]
Across surveyed sectors, organisations that have integrated AI productivity tools report measurable gains in routine task completion — often in the range of fifteen to thirty per cent — but smaller and more variable gains in tasks requiring judgement. Where deployment has been accompanied by deliberate redesign of workflows and reskilling investment, outcomes have been substantially better than where the tools were simply added to existing processes. The most common implementation failure observed is the assumption that productivity gains will accrue automatically from the technology itself, independent of how work is restructured around it.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Union submission to a labour committee]
Members report that the introduction of AI tools has been used, in some cases, as a justification for reduced staffing, narrower job descriptions, and heavier expectations of output per remaining worker. Where AI is deployed as a productivity aid, the results have been positive and the workforce has, on the whole, welcomed it. Where AI is deployed as a headcount-reduction strategy, the results have been negative for both workers and, on members' reports, for service quality. The case for regulation is not a case against AI itself. It is a case against leaving the framing of its deployment entirely to the side that benefits from cost reduction.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Academic analysis]
The literature on technological change and employment is older than the current AI debate and offers consistent patterns. Productivity-enhancing technologies have rarely produced net job losses at the aggregate level, but they have consistently produced redistribution — of work, of wages, and of bargaining power. Whether the redistribution serves the broader economy depends on policy choices made around the technology, not on the technology itself. The debate cast as 'AI versus jobs' is therefore miscast. The genuine question is who captures the gains, under what conditions, and with what obligations to those displaced — a question that applies as readily to the spinning jenny as to a large language model.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Planning economist]
The argument for higher urban density rests on three empirical claims that have, in the main, withstood scrutiny: denser cities use less energy per capita; denser cities support more public transport at lower subsidy per ride; denser cities concentrate the agglomeration effects associated with innovation and wage growth. The argument against — that density produces congestion, pollution, and social strain — tends to confuse correlation with causation. Most of the negative consequences attributed to density are, on closer examination, consequences of under-investment in the infrastructure that density requires.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Letter from a longtime resident]
I have lived on this street for thirty-seven years. When I arrived, it had houses and gardens and children. The planners' argument now is that we should welcome higher buildings because density is good for the environment and for the economy. I do not dispute either claim. I observe that my street has not been consulted on whether the density should happen to it specifically, or on what would happen to the children. I observe that the planners do not live on this street, and will not, when the density is built. The arguments for density may be sound. The way they are being deployed against particular communities is a separate question.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Comparative case study]
Comparison of two mid-sized cities — one that increased density steadily over two decades through neighbourhood-scale changes, and one that introduced high-rise development rapidly in a small number of designated zones — suggests that the pace and geography of densification matter as much as its overall level. The slow-and-distributed city retained stronger neighbourhood ties and showed less displacement of long-standing residents. The rapid-and-zoned city reached its density targets faster but produced greater social friction and more vocal resistance. Both cities are now denser than they were; only one is recognisably the community it had previously been.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Agricultural economist's note]
The case for direct income support during prolonged drought, rather than subsidy of inputs, rests on a consistent finding across reviews of rural policy: subsidies on seed, feed, or water tend to be capitalised into land values and recovered, in time, by landowners rather than by working farmers. Direct cash transfers, by contrast, reach the household and are spent on the household's specific bottleneck. The argument against direct transfers — that they discourage adaptation — is not strongly supported by recent evidence. Adaptation appears to depend on adaptive capacity, which is constrained by liquidity. Constraining liquidity to force adaptation is a strategy that has not, on the evidence, produced the adaptation it was meant to.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: A farmer's testimony]
The third year of drought is when the policy people stop arriving. The first year they come with cameras. The second year with forms. By the third year the only people still arriving are the ones with offers to buy your land. I do not say this because I distrust policy research. I say it because the people writing the research are not the people the research was meant to describe. We have outlived our usefulness as a story. The decisions are being made elsewhere now, by people who have written down what we said in the first year and who have, since then, moved on to whatever the next first year is going to be.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: NGO field report]
Field observations across three drought-affected districts suggest that household-level resilience is shaped less by the size of any single intervention than by the predictability of the support over time. Households that knew, in advance, that a given form of support would continue for at least eighteen months made different decisions than households facing the same support delivered as a one-off. The implication for policy is uncomfortable. Short-term emergency relief, however generous, may produce worse long-term outcomes than smaller but predictable medium-term support — a finding that contradicts the emergency framing under which most current programmes are designed and funded.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Industry consultancy report]
Across surveyed sectors, organisations that have integrated AI productivity tools report measurable gains in routine task completion — often in the range of fifteen to thirty per cent — but smaller and more variable gains in tasks requiring judgement. Where deployment has been accompanied by deliberate redesign of workflows and reskilling investment, outcomes have been substantially better than where the tools were simply added to existing processes. The most common implementation failure observed is the assumption that productivity gains will accrue automatically from the technology itself, independent of how work is restructured around it.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Union submission to a labour committee]
Members report that the introduction of AI tools has been used, in some cases, as a justification for reduced staffing, narrower job descriptions, and heavier expectations of output per remaining worker. Where AI is deployed as a productivity aid, the results have been positive and the workforce has, on the whole, welcomed it. Where AI is deployed as a headcount-reduction strategy, the results have been negative for both workers and, on members' reports, for service quality. The case for regulation is not a case against AI itself. It is a case against leaving the framing of its deployment entirely to the side that benefits from cost reduction.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Academic analysis]
The literature on technological change and employment is older than the current AI debate and offers consistent patterns. Productivity-enhancing technologies have rarely produced net job losses at the aggregate level, but they have consistently produced redistribution — of work, of wages, and of bargaining power. Whether the redistribution serves the broader economy depends on policy choices made around the technology, not on the technology itself. The debate cast as 'AI versus jobs' is therefore miscast. The genuine question is who captures the gains, under what conditions, and with what obligations to those displaced — a question that applies as readily to the spinning jenny as to a large language model.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Planning economist]
The argument for higher urban density rests on three empirical claims that have, in the main, withstood scrutiny: denser cities use less energy per capita; denser cities support more public transport at lower subsidy per ride; denser cities concentrate the agglomeration effects associated with innovation and wage growth. The argument against — that density produces congestion, pollution, and social strain — tends to confuse correlation with causation. Most of the negative consequences attributed to density are, on closer examination, consequences of under-investment in the infrastructure that density requires.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Letter from a longtime resident]
I have lived on this street for thirty-seven years. When I arrived, it had houses and gardens and children. The planners' argument now is that we should welcome higher buildings because density is good for the environment and for the economy. I do not dispute either claim. I observe that my street has not been consulted on whether the density should happen to it specifically, or on what would happen to the children. I observe that the planners do not live on this street, and will not, when the density is built. The arguments for density may be sound. The way they are being deployed against particular communities is a separate question.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Comparative case study]
Comparison of two mid-sized cities — one that increased density steadily over two decades through neighbourhood-scale changes, and one that introduced high-rise development rapidly in a small number of designated zones — suggests that the pace and geography of densification matter as much as its overall level. The slow-and-distributed city retained stronger neighbourhood ties and showed less displacement of long-standing residents. The rapid-and-zoned city reached its density targets faster but produced greater social friction and more vocal resistance. Both cities are now denser than they were; only one is recognisably the community it had previously been.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Agricultural economist's note]
The case for direct income support during prolonged drought, rather than subsidy of inputs, rests on a consistent finding across reviews of rural policy: subsidies on seed, feed, or water tend to be capitalised into land values and recovered, in time, by landowners rather than by working farmers. Direct cash transfers, by contrast, reach the household and are spent on the household's specific bottleneck. The argument against direct transfers — that they discourage adaptation — is not strongly supported by recent evidence. Adaptation appears to depend on adaptive capacity, which is constrained by liquidity. Constraining liquidity to force adaptation is a strategy that has not, on the evidence, produced the adaptation it was meant to.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: A farmer's testimony]

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Industry consultancy report]
Across surveyed sectors, organisations that have integrated AI productivity tools report measurable gains in routine task completion — often in the range of fifteen to thirty per cent — but smaller and more variable gains in tasks requiring judgement. Where deployment has been accompanied by deliberate redesign of workflows and reskilling investment, outcomes have been substantially better than where the tools were simply added to existing processes. The most common implementation failure observed is the assumption that productivity gains will accrue automatically from the technology itself, independent of how work is restructured around it.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Union submission to a labour committee]
Members report that the introduction of AI tools has been used, in some cases, as a justification for reduced staffing, narrower job descriptions, and heavier expectations of output per remaining worker. Where AI is deployed as a productivity aid, the results have been positive and the workforce has, on the whole, welcomed it. Where AI is deployed as a headcount-reduction strategy, the results have been negative for both workers and, on members' reports, for service quality. The case for regulation is not a case against AI itself. It is a case against leaving the framing of its deployment entirely to the side that benefits from cost reduction.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Academic analysis]
The literature on technological change and employment is older than the current AI debate and offers consistent patterns. Productivity-enhancing technologies have rarely produced net job losses at the aggregate level, but they have consistently produced redistribution — of work, of wages, and of bargaining power. Whether the redistribution serves the broader economy depends on policy choices made around the technology, not on the technology itself. The debate cast as 'AI versus jobs' is therefore miscast. The genuine question is who captures the gains, under what conditions, and with what obligations to those displaced — a question that applies as readily to the spinning jenny as to a large language model.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Planning economist]
The argument for higher urban density rests on three empirical claims that have, in the main, withstood scrutiny: denser cities use less energy per capita; denser cities support more public transport at lower subsidy per ride; denser cities concentrate the agglomeration effects associated with innovation and wage growth. The argument against — that density produces congestion, pollution, and social strain — tends to confuse correlation with causation. Most of the negative consequences attributed to density are, on closer examination, consequences of under-investment in the infrastructure that density requires.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Letter from a longtime resident]
I have lived on this street for thirty-seven years. When I arrived, it had houses and gardens and children. The planners' argument now is that we should welcome higher buildings because density is good for the environment and for the economy. I do not dispute either claim. I observe that my street has not been consulted on whether the density should happen to it specifically, or on what would happen to the children. I observe that the planners do not live on this street, and will not, when the density is built. The arguments for density may be sound. The way they are being deployed against particular communities is a separate question.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Comparative case study]
Comparison of two mid-sized cities — one that increased density steadily over two decades through neighbourhood-scale changes, and one that introduced high-rise development rapidly in a small number of designated zones — suggests that the pace and geography of densification matter as much as its overall level. The slow-and-distributed city retained stronger neighbourhood ties and showed less displacement of long-standing residents. The rapid-and-zoned city reached its density targets faster but produced greater social friction and more vocal resistance. Both cities are now denser than they were; only one is recognisably the community it had previously been.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Agricultural economist's note]
The case for direct income support during prolonged drought, rather than subsidy of inputs, rests on a consistent finding across reviews of rural policy: subsidies on seed, feed, or water tend to be capitalised into land values and recovered, in time, by landowners rather than by working farmers. Direct cash transfers, by contrast, reach the household and are spent on the household's specific bottleneck. The argument against direct transfers — that they discourage adaptation — is not strongly supported by recent evidence. Adaptation appears to depend on adaptive capacity, which is constrained by liquidity. Constraining liquidity to force adaptation is a strategy that has not, on the evidence, produced the adaptation it was meant to.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: A farmer's testimony]
The third year of drought is when the policy people stop arriving. The first year they come with cameras. The second year with forms. By the third year the only people still arriving are the ones with offers to buy your land. I do not say this because I distrust policy research. I say it because the people writing the research are not the people the research was meant to describe. We have outlived our usefulness as a story. The decisions are being made elsewhere now, by people who have written down what we said in the first year and who have, since then, moved on to whatever the next first year is going to be.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: NGO field report]
Field observations across three drought-affected districts suggest that household-level resilience is shaped less by the size of any single intervention than by the predictability of the support over time. Households that knew, in advance, that a given form of support would continue for at least eighteen months made different decisions than households facing the same support delivered as a one-off. The implication for policy is uncomfortable. Short-term emergency relief, however generous, may produce worse long-term outcomes than smaller but predictable medium-term support — a finding that contradicts the emergency framing under which most current programmes are designed and funded.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Industry consultancy report]
Across surveyed sectors, organisations that have integrated AI productivity tools report measurable gains in routine task completion — often in the range of fifteen to thirty per cent — but smaller and more variable gains in tasks requiring judgement. Where deployment has been accompanied by deliberate redesign of workflows and reskilling investment, outcomes have been substantially better than where the tools were simply added to existing processes. The most common implementation failure observed is the assumption that productivity gains will accrue automatically from the technology itself, independent of how work is restructured around it.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Union submission to a labour committee]
Members report that the introduction of AI tools has been used, in some cases, as a justification for reduced staffing, narrower job descriptions, and heavier expectations of output per remaining worker. Where AI is deployed as a productivity aid, the results have been positive and the workforce has, on the whole, welcomed it. Where AI is deployed as a headcount-reduction strategy, the results have been negative for both workers and, on members' reports, for service quality. The case for regulation is not a case against AI itself. It is a case against leaving the framing of its deployment entirely to the side that benefits from cost reduction.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Academic analysis]
The literature on technological change and employment is older than the current AI debate and offers consistent patterns. Productivity-enhancing technologies have rarely produced net job losses at the aggregate level, but they have consistently produced redistribution — of work, of wages, and of bargaining power. Whether the redistribution serves the broader economy depends on policy choices made around the technology, not on the technology itself. The debate cast as 'AI versus jobs' is therefore miscast. The genuine question is who captures the gains, under what conditions, and with what obligations to those displaced — a question that applies as readily to the spinning jenny as to a large language model.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Planning economist]
The argument for higher urban density rests on three empirical claims that have, in the main, withstood scrutiny: denser cities use less energy per capita; denser cities support more public transport at lower subsidy per ride; denser cities concentrate the agglomeration effects associated with innovation and wage growth. The argument against — that density produces congestion, pollution, and social strain — tends to confuse correlation with causation. Most of the negative consequences attributed to density are, on closer examination, consequences of under-investment in the infrastructure that density requires.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Letter from a longtime resident]
I have lived on this street for thirty-seven years. When I arrived, it had houses and gardens and children. The planners' argument now is that we should welcome higher buildings because density is good for the environment and for the economy. I do not dispute either claim. I observe that my street has not been consulted on whether the density should happen to it specifically, or on what would happen to the children. I observe that the planners do not live on this street, and will not, when the density is built. The arguments for density may be sound. The way they are being deployed against particular communities is a separate question.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Comparative case study]
Comparison of two mid-sized cities — one that increased density steadily over two decades through neighbourhood-scale changes, and one that introduced high-rise development rapidly in a small number of designated zones — suggests that the pace and geography of densification matter as much as its overall level. The slow-and-distributed city retained stronger neighbourhood ties and showed less displacement of long-standing residents. The rapid-and-zoned city reached its density targets faster but produced greater social friction and more vocal resistance. Both cities are now denser than they were; only one is recognisably the community it had previously been.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Agricultural economist's note]
The case for direct income support during prolonged drought, rather than subsidy of inputs, rests on a consistent finding across reviews of rural policy: subsidies on seed, feed, or water tend to be capitalised into land values and recovered, in time, by landowners rather than by working farmers. Direct cash transfers, by contrast, reach the household and are spent on the household's specific bottleneck. The argument against direct transfers — that they discourage adaptation — is not strongly supported by recent evidence. Adaptation appears to depend on adaptive capacity, which is constrained by liquidity. Constraining liquidity to force adaptation is a strategy that has not, on the evidence, produced the adaptation it was meant to.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: A farmer's testimony]
The third year of drought is when the policy people stop arriving. The first year they come with cameras. The second year with forms. By the third year the only people still arriving are the ones with offers to buy your land. I do not say this because I distrust policy research. I say it because the people writing the research are not the people the research was meant to describe. We have outlived our usefulness as a story. The decisions are being made elsewhere now, by people who have written down what we said in the first year and who have, since then, moved on to whatever the next first year is going to be.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: NGO field report]
Field observations across three drought-affected districts suggest that household-level resilience is shaped less by the size of any single intervention than by the predictability of the support over time. Households that knew, in advance, that a given form of support would continue for at least eighteen months made different decisions than households facing the same support delivered as a one-off. The implication for policy is uncomfortable. Short-term emergency relief, however generous, may produce worse long-term outcomes than smaller but predictable medium-term support — a finding that contradicts the emergency framing under which most current programmes are designed and funded.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Industry consultancy report]
Across surveyed sectors, organisations that have integrated AI productivity tools report measurable gains in routine task completion — often in the range of fifteen to thirty per cent — but smaller and more variable gains in tasks requiring judgement. Where deployment has been accompanied by deliberate redesign of workflows and reskilling investment, outcomes have been substantially better than where the tools were simply added to existing processes. The most common implementation failure observed is the assumption that productivity gains will accrue automatically from the technology itself, independent of how work is restructured around it.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Union submission to a labour committee]
Members report that the introduction of AI tools has been used, in some cases, as a justification for reduced staffing, narrower job descriptions, and heavier expectations of output per remaining worker. Where AI is deployed as a productivity aid, the results have been positive and the workforce has, on the whole, welcomed it. Where AI is deployed as a headcount-reduction strategy, the results have been negative for both workers and, on members' reports, for service quality. The case for regulation is not a case against AI itself. It is a case against leaving the framing of its deployment entirely to the side that benefits from cost reduction.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Academic analysis]
The literature on technological change and employment is older than the current AI debate and offers consistent patterns. Productivity-enhancing technologies have rarely produced net job losses at the aggregate level, but they have consistently produced redistribution — of work, of wages, and of bargaining power. Whether the redistribution serves the broader economy depends on policy choices made around the technology, not on the technology itself. The debate cast as 'AI versus jobs' is therefore miscast. The genuine question is who captures the gains, under what conditions, and with what obligations to those displaced — a question that applies as readily to the spinning jenny as to a large language model.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Planning economist]
The argument for higher urban density rests on three empirical claims that have, in the main, withstood scrutiny: denser cities use less energy per capita; denser cities support more public transport at lower subsidy per ride; denser cities concentrate the agglomeration effects associated with innovation and wage growth. The argument against — that density produces congestion, pollution, and social strain — tends to confuse correlation with causation. Most of the negative consequences attributed to density are, on closer examination, consequences of under-investment in the infrastructure that density requires.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Letter from a longtime resident]
I have lived on this street for thirty-seven years. When I arrived, it had houses and gardens and children. The planners' argument now is that we should welcome higher buildings because density is good for the environment and for the economy. I do not dispute either claim. I observe that my street has not been consulted on whether the density should happen to it specifically, or on what would happen to the children. I observe that the planners do not live on this street, and will not, when the density is built. The arguments for density may be sound. The way they are being deployed against particular communities is a separate question.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Comparative case study]
Comparison of two mid-sized cities — one that increased density steadily over two decades through neighbourhood-scale changes, and one that introduced high-rise development rapidly in a small number of designated zones — suggests that the pace and geography of densification matter as much as its overall level. The slow-and-distributed city retained stronger neighbourhood ties and showed less displacement of long-standing residents. The rapid-and-zoned city reached its density targets faster but produced greater social friction and more vocal resistance. Both cities are now denser than they were; only one is recognisably the community it had previously been.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Agricultural economist's note]
The case for direct income support during prolonged drought, rather than subsidy of inputs, rests on a consistent finding across reviews of rural policy: subsidies on seed, feed, or water tend to be capitalised into land values and recovered, in time, by landowners rather than by working farmers. Direct cash transfers, by contrast, reach the household and are spent on the household's specific bottleneck. The argument against direct transfers — that they discourage adaptation — is not strongly supported by recent evidence. Adaptation appears to depend on adaptive capacity, which is constrained by liquidity. Constraining liquidity to force adaptation is a strategy that has not, on the evidence, produced the adaptation it was meant to.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: A farmer's testimony]
The third year of drought is when the policy people stop arriving. The first year they come with cameras. The second year with forms. By the third year the only people still arriving are the ones with offers to buy your land. I do not say this because I distrust policy research. I say it because the people writing the research are not the people the research was meant to describe. We have outlived our usefulness as a story. The decisions are being made elsewhere now, by people who have written down what we said in the first year and who have, since then, moved on to whatever the next first year is going to be.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: NGO field report]
Field observations across three drought-affected districts suggest that household-level resilience is shaped less by the size of any single intervention than by the predictability of the support over time. Households that knew, in advance, that a given form of support would continue for at least eighteen months made different decisions than households facing the same support delivered as a one-off. The implication for policy is uncomfortable. Short-term emergency relief, however generous, may produce worse long-term outcomes than smaller but predictable medium-term support — a finding that contradicts the emergency framing under which most current programmes are designed and funded.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Industry consultancy report]
Across surveyed sectors, organisations that have integrated AI productivity tools report measurable gains in routine task completion — often in the range of fifteen to thirty per cent — but smaller and more variable gains in tasks requiring judgement. Where deployment has been accompanied by deliberate redesign of workflows and reskilling investment, outcomes have been substantially better than where the tools were simply added to existing processes. The most common implementation failure observed is the assumption that productivity gains will accrue automatically from the technology itself, independent of how work is restructured around it.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Union submission to a labour committee]
Members report that the introduction of AI tools has been used, in some cases, as a justification for reduced staffing, narrower job descriptions, and heavier expectations of output per remaining worker. Where AI is deployed as a productivity aid, the results have been positive and the workforce has, on the whole, welcomed it. Where AI is deployed as a headcount-reduction strategy, the results have been negative for both workers and, on members' reports, for service quality. The case for regulation is not a case against AI itself. It is a case against leaving the framing of its deployment entirely to the side that benefits from cost reduction.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Academic analysis]
The literature on technological change and employment is older than the current AI debate and offers consistent patterns. Productivity-enhancing technologies have rarely produced net job losses at the aggregate level, but they have consistently produced redistribution — of work, of wages, and of bargaining power. Whether the redistribution serves the broader economy depends on policy choices made around the technology, not on the technology itself. The debate cast as 'AI versus jobs' is therefore miscast. The genuine question is who captures the gains, under what conditions, and with what obligations to those displaced — a question that applies as readily to the spinning jenny as to a large language model.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Planning economist]
The argument for higher urban density rests on three empirical claims that have, in the main, withstood scrutiny: denser cities use less energy per capita; denser cities support more public transport at lower subsidy per ride; denser cities concentrate the agglomeration effects associated with innovation and wage growth. The argument against — that density produces congestion, pollution, and social strain — tends to confuse correlation with causation. Most of the negative consequences attributed to density are, on closer examination, consequences of under-investment in the infrastructure that density requires.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Letter from a longtime resident]
I have lived on this street for thirty-seven years. When I arrived, it had houses and gardens and children. The planners' argument now is that we should welcome higher buildings because density is good for the environment and for the economy. I do not dispute either claim. I observe that my street has not been consulted on whether the density should happen to it specifically, or on what would happen to the children. I observe that the planners do not live on this street, and will not, when the density is built. The arguments for density may be sound. The way they are being deployed against particular communities is a separate question.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Comparative case study]
Comparison of two mid-sized cities — one that increased density steadily over two decades through neighbourhood-scale changes, and one that introduced high-rise development rapidly in a small number of designated zones — suggests that the pace and geography of densification matter as much as its overall level. The slow-and-distributed city retained stronger neighbourhood ties and showed less displacement of long-standing residents. The rapid-and-zoned city reached its density targets faster but produced greater social friction and more vocal resistance. Both cities are now denser than they were; only one is recognisably the community it had previously been.

items.passage:
=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Agricultural economist's note]
The case for direct income support during prolonged drought, rather than subsidy of inputs, rests on a consistent finding across reviews of rural policy: subsidies on seed, feed, or water tend to be capitalised into land values and recovered, in time, by landowners rather than by working farmers. Direct cash transfers, by contrast, reach the household and are spent on the household's specific bottleneck. The argument against direct transfers — that they discourage adaptation — is not strongly supported by recent evidence. Adaptation appears to depend on adaptive capacity, which is constrained by liquidity. Constraining liquidity to force adaptation is a strategy that has not, on the evidence, produced the adaptation it was meant to.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: A farmer's testimony]
The third year of drought is when the policy people stop arriving. The first year they come with cameras. The second year with forms. By the third year the only people still arriving are the ones with offers to buy your land. I do not say this because I distrust policy research. I say it because the people writing the research are not the people the research was meant to describe. We have outlived our usefulness as a story. The decisions are being made elsewhere now, by people who have written down what we said in the first year and who have, since then, moved on to whatever the next first year is going to be.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: NGO field report]
Field observations across three drought-affected districts suggest that household-level resilience is shaped less by the size of any single intervention than by the predictability of the support over time. Households that knew, in advance, that a given form of support would continue for at least eighteen months made different decisions than households facing the same support delivered as a one-off. The implication for policy is uncomfortable. Short-term emergency relief, however generous, may produce worse long-term outcomes than smaller but predictable medium-term support — a finding that contradicts the emergency framing under which most current programmes are designed and funded.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Industry consultancy report]
Across surveyed sectors, organisations that have integrated AI productivity tools report measurable gains in routine task completion — often in the range of fifteen to thirty per cent — but smaller and more variable gains in tasks requiring judgement. Where deployment has been accompanied by deliberate redesign of workflows and reskilling investment, outcomes have been substantially better than where the tools were simply added to existing processes. The most common implementation failure observed is the assumption that productivity gains will accrue automatically from the technology itself, independent of how work is restructured around it.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Union submission to a labour committee]
Members report that the introduction of AI tools has been used, in some cases, as a justification for reduced staffing, narrower job descriptions, and heavier expectations of output per remaining worker. Where AI is deployed as a productivity aid, the results have been positive and the workforce has, on the whole, welcomed it. Where AI is deployed as a headcount-reduction strategy, the results have been negative for both workers and, on members' reports, for service quality. The case for regulation is not a case against AI itself. It is a case against leaving the framing of its deployment entirely to the side that benefits from cost reduction.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Academic analysis]
The literature on technological change and employment is older than the current AI debate and offers consistent patterns. Productivity-enhancing technologies have rarely produced net job losses at the aggregate level, but they have consistently produced redistribution — of work, of wages, and of bargaining power. Whether the redistribution serves the broader economy depends on policy choices made around the technology, not on the technology itself. The debate cast as 'AI versus jobs' is therefore miscast. The genuine question is who captures the gains, under what conditions, and with what obligations to those displaced — a question that applies as readily to the spinning jenny as to a large language model.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Planning economist]
The argument for higher urban density rests on three empirical claims that have, in the main, withstood scrutiny: denser cities use less energy per capita; denser cities support more public transport at lower subsidy per ride; denser cities concentrate the agglomeration effects associated with innovation and wage growth. The argument against — that density produces congestion, pollution, and social strain — tends to confuse correlation with causation. Most of the negative consequences attributed to density are, on closer examination, consequences of under-investment in the infrastructure that density requires.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: Letter from a longtime resident]
I have lived on this street for thirty-seven years. When I arrived, it had houses and gardens and children. The planners' argument now is that we should welcome higher buildings because density is good for the environment and for the economy. I do not dispute either claim. I observe that my street has not been consulted on whether the density should happen to it specifically, or on what would happen to the children. I observe that the planners do not live on this street, and will not, when the density is built. The arguments for density may be sound. The way they are being deployed against particular communities is a separate question.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: Comparative case study]
Comparison of two mid-sized cities — one that increased density steadily over two decades through neighbourhood-scale changes, and one that introduced high-rise development rapidly in a small number of designated zones — suggests that the pace and geography of densification matter as much as its overall level. The slow-and-distributed city retained stronger neighbourhood ties and showed less displacement of long-standing residents. The rapid-and-zoned city reached its density targets faster but produced greater social friction and more vocal resistance. Both cities are now denser than they were; only one is recognisably the community it had previously been.

=== Source 1 ===
[Source 1: Agricultural economist's note]
The case for direct income support during prolonged drought, rather than subsidy of inputs, rests on a consistent finding across reviews of rural policy: subsidies on seed, feed, or water tend to be capitalised into land values and recovered, in time, by landowners rather than by working farmers. Direct cash transfers, by contrast, reach the household and are spent on the household's specific bottleneck. The argument against direct transfers — that they discourage adaptation — is not strongly supported by recent evidence. Adaptation appears to depend on adaptive capacity, which is constrained by liquidity. Constraining liquidity to force adaptation is a strategy that has not, on the evidence, produced the adaptation it was meant to.

=== Source 2 ===
[Source 2: A farmer's testimony]
The third year of drought is when the policy people stop arriving. The first year they come with cameras. The second year with forms. By the third year the only people still arriving are the ones with offers to buy your land. I do not say this because I distrust policy research. I say it because the people writing the research are not the people the research was meant to describe. We have outlived our usefulness as a story. The decisions are being made elsewhere now, by people who have written down what we said in the first year and who have, since then, moved on to whatever the next first year is going to be.

=== Source 3 ===
[Source 3: NGO field report]
Field observations across three drought-affected districts suggest that household-level resilience is shaped less by the size of any single intervention than by the predictability of the support over time. Households that knew, in advance, that a given form of support would continue for at least eighteen months made different decisions than households facing the same support delivered as a one-off. The implication for policy is uncomfortable. Short-term emergency relief, however generous, may produce worse long-term outcomes than smaller but predictable medium-term support — a finding that contradicts the emergency framing under which most current programmes are designed and funded.

Scenario: You are applicant for a national academic scholarship. Five interviewers ask you the following challenging questions. Answer each in 80–120 words.

  Q1. What is the most significant difference between what you knew about your chosen field a year ago and what you know now?
  Q2. Describe a time you held an academic position that turned out to be wrong. How did you discover it?
  Q3. If we offered this scholarship to a slightly less qualified applicant who would benefit from it more, would we be wrong to do so?
  Q4. What is the limit of what this scholarship can do for someone like you?
  Q5. Why should the decision be a yes — when there are many applicants who would also benefit?

Your answers must: (1) demonstrate evaluative thinking — not factual recall; (2) include self-awareness in at least 2 answers; (3) include a specific example in at least 4 of 5 answers; (4) maintain consistent tone — same candidate; (5) use formal interview register; (6) include at least 1 integrative answer that refers back to a previous answer.

items.prompt:
Scenario: You are applicant for a postgraduate research position. Five interviewers ask you the following challenging questions. Answer each in 80–120 words.

  Q1. What is the most important question in your field that is currently being asked poorly?
  Q2. Describe a time you abandoned a project that was working in order to start a better one. What did you lose?
  Q3. Why this supervisor specifically? What would you not get from a different supervisor?
  Q4. If your research succeeds, what would the field look like in five years?
  Q5. If it fails, what will you have learned that you could not have learned without trying?

Your answers must: (1) demonstrate evaluative thinking — not factual recall; (2) include self-awareness in at least 2 answers; (3) include a specific example in at least 4 of 5 answers; (4) maintain consistent tone — same candidate; (5) use formal interview register; (6) include at least 1 integrative answer that refers back to a previous answer.

  Q5. If it fails, what will you have learned that you could not have learned without trying?

  Q1. What is the most significant difference between what you knew about your chosen field a year ago and what you know now?
  Q2. Describe a time you held an academic position that turned out to be wrong. How did you discover it?
  Q3. If we offered this scholarship to a slightly less qualified applicant who would benefit from it more, would we be wrong to do so?
  Q4. What is the limit of what this scholarship can do for someone like you?
  Q5. Why should the decision be a yes — when there are many applicants who would also benefit?

Your answers must: (1) demonstrate evaluative thinking — not factual recall; (2) include self-awareness in at least 2 answers; (3) include a specific example in at least 4 of 5 answers; (4) maintain consistent tone — same candidate; (5) use formal interview register; (6) include at least 1 integrative answer that refers back to a previous answer.

items.stimulus:
Scenario: You are applicant for a postgraduate research position. Five interviewers ask you the following challenging questions. Answer each in 80–120 words.

  Q1. What is the most important question in your field that is currently being asked poorly?
  Q2. Describe a time you abandoned a project that was working in order to start a better one. What did you lose?
  Q3. Why this supervisor specifically? What would you not get from a different supervisor?
  Q4. If your research succeeds, what would the field look like in five years?
  Q5. If it fails, what will you have learned that you could not have learned without trying?

Your answers must: (1) demonstrate evaluative thinking — not factual recall; (2) include self-awareness in at least 2 answers; (3) include a specific example in at least 4 of 5 answers; (4) maintain consistent tone — same candidate; (5) use formal interview register; (6) include at least 1 integrative answer that refers back to a previous answer.

Scenario: You are candidate for a national youth leadership council seat. Five interviewers ask you the following challenging questions. Answer each in 80–120 words.

  Q1. What is one widely held view about young people that you think is wrong?

  Q5. What is the smallest meaningful change this council could make in the next twelve months?

  Q1. What did you understand about research before you began applying that you no longer believe?

  Q2. Describe a time when an apparent strength of yours turned out to be a limitation.
  Q3. Why this institution specifically? What would you not get from a comparable institution closer to home?
  Q4. How will you carry your home community into the work you do there?
  Q5. What is the question we should be asking you that we have not?

Your answers must: (1) demonstrate evaluative thinking — not factual recall; (2) include self-awareness in at least 2 answers; (3) include a specific example in at least 4 of 5 answers; (4) maintain consistent tone — same candidate; (5) use formal interview register; (6) include at least 1 integrative answer that refers back to a previous answer. At Hard difficulty, your fifth answer should reveal a depth of thought the panel could not have anticipated from your first four — not by contradiction, but by extension.

Task: Answer all 5 panel questions at 80–120 words each (total 400–600 words).

Tone consistent across all 5 answers.
Formal interview register sustained — no slang, no fillers, no contractions.
Each answer 80–120 words.
At least 1 answer integrates or refers back to a prior answer — demonstrating a coherent candidate, not 5 isolated responses.

items.prompt:
Venue: a global climate summit youth panel.
Topic: Why climate adaptation is not a technical problem but a moral one.

Write a persuasive speech at DISTINCTION level (500–700 words, approximately 5–6 minutes spoken). alternateValidPatterns.name: subtle-interpretation
alternateValidPatterns.description: Interpretations carried by sustained tone, image, or framing — rather than declarative thesis sentences — are valid when the textual basis is identifiable.

alternateValidPatterns.name: restrained-literary-analysis
alternateValidPatterns.description: Few techniques unpacked at depth is preferable to many techniques listed without unpacking.

alternateValidPatterns.name: non-template-reasoning
alternateValidPatterns.description: Non-five-paragraph structure is valid where each rubric function is performed at some location in the essay.

alternateValidPatterns.name: implicit-rebuttal-logic
alternateValidPatterns.description: A rebuttal whose logic is implicit in evidence selection or framing counts as a rebuttal when the implicit claim is recoverable from the prose.

alternateValidPatterns.name: layered-without-overt-labels

alternateValidPatterns.name: unconventional-but-coherent-structure

items.prompt:
Venue: a youth leadership conference.
Topic: Why young people should expect to lead, not merely to participate.

Write a persuasive speech at DISTINCTION level (500–700 words, approximately 5–6 minutes spoken). Your speech must: (1) open with a rhetorical device (anaphora, rhetorical question, anecdote, antithesis, surprising claim); (2) develop a LAYERED argument — main position + supporting layer + counterpoint + resolved tension; (3) acknowledge the counterpoint in its STRONGEST form, then engage; (4) resolve the tension at a level that holds both partially valid; (5) deploy at least 3 distinct rhetorical techniques; (6) maintain direct address to the specific audience; (7) close with a call that invites occupation of a position — not just an action item; (8) sustain formal-spoken register at distinction level.

Venue: a national reading week launch.
Topic: Why the reading habit is the slowest-acting and most important form of citizenship.

Write a persuasive speech at DISTINCTION level (500–700 words, approximately 5–6 minutes spoken). items.prompt:
Venue: a public library re-opening.
Topic: Why a library is a promise, not a service.

Write a persuasive speech at DISTINCTION level (500–700 words, approximately 5–6 minutes spoken). Your speech must: (1) open with a rhetorical device (anaphora, rhetorical question, anecdote, antithesis, surprising claim); (2) develop a LAYERED argument — main position + supporting layer + counterpoint + resolved tension; (3) acknowledge the counterpoint in its STRONGEST form, then engage; (4) resolve the tension at a level that holds both partially valid; (5) deploy at least 3 distinct rhetorical techniques; (6) maintain direct address to the specific audience; (7) close with a call that invites occupation of a position — not just an action item; (8) sustain formal-spoken register at distinction level. At Hard difficulty, the speech should end with the audience holding a more complex position than it began with — not a simpler one.
